subtopics.title: Compilation Model — Translation Units, Preprocessing, ODR
subtopics.explanation:
A translation unit is the basic unit of compilation in C++. It consists of a source file (.cpp) along with all the headers it includes (directly or transitively), after preprocessing. The preprocessor handles `#include directives` (textual inclusion), `#define macros`, conditional compilation (`#ifdef`/`#ifndef`/`#if`), and other directives before the compiler sees the code.

The **One Definition Rule** (**ODR**) states that every entity (variable, function, class, `template`) must have exactly one definition in the entire program, though it may have multiple declarations. Inline functions and templates are exceptions — they may be defined in multiple translation units, but all definitions must be identical (token-for-token). **ODR** violations are undefined behavior and usually not diagnosed by the compiler.

The compilation model means each .cpp file is compiled independently into an object file (.o/.obj). The linker then combines these object files, resolving symbol references across translation units. This is why you declare functions in headers but define them in source files — to avoid multiple definitions.

### Unforgettable Analogy / Deep Dive
Think of building a C++ program like baking a layered cake from a recipe book:
- **`Preprocessing**` is like preparing the ingredients: reading the recipe, getting the tools ready, and copying text from your shopping list (replacing `#include` with actual header text).
- **`Compilation**` is like baking each layer of the cake (translation units) independently into object files (`.o`/`.obj`). The compiler doesn't know about other layers yet; it just compiles one source file at a time.
- **`Linking**` is assembling the layers together. The linker checks if any layers are missing and ensures that there is only exactly one recipe definition (**`ODR**`) for each layer.
- ****One Definition Rule** (**ODR**)** prevents multiple co-authors from defining different recipes for the same layer. If one author defines `LayerA` with chocolate and another with vanilla, the editor gets confused and you get Undefined Behavior.

questions.question: What is a translation unit?
questions.answer: A translation unit is a source file after preprocessing — the .cpp file with all #includes expanded, macros substituted, and conditional compilation resolved. It is the unit that the compiler processes independently.

questions.question: What is the One Definition Rule?
questions.answer: ODR says every used entity must have exactly one definition in the program. Inline functions and templates may have multiple definitions across TUs if they're all identical. Violating ODR is undefined behavior.

questions.question: Why can't you put function definitions in headers?
questions.answer: If a non-inline function is defined in a header and included by multiple .cpp files, each TU gets a definition, causing a linker 'multiple definition' error. Use inline keyword or define in a single .cpp file.

mcqs.question: What is the exact outcome of violating the One Definition Rule (ODR) for an entity across different translation units in C++ when studying `Compilation Model — Translation Units, Preprocessing, ODR`?
options: The compiler will fail to compile with a duplicate definition error.
The linker will always fail to link with a multiple definition error.
The program compiles and links successfully, but triggers Undefined Behavior at runtime.
The program is guaranteed to run correctly if all optimizations are disabled.
mcqs.explanation: ODR violations across different translation units are undefined behavior (UB). Linkers are not required to diagnose them, and they often silently select one definition, leading to random runtime crashes or wrong results.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a translation unit in C++?
options: A single `.cpp` file after preprocessing (with headers expanded).
An individual `.h` header file compiled by itself as a source.
A source file with all its included headers, after macros have been replaced.
A temporary preprocessed file (`.i`) generated by the compiler's preprocessor.
mcqs.explanation: A header file by itself is not a translation unit. A translation unit is a source file (.cpp, .cc) with all its included headers expanded by the preprocessor.

mcqs.question: What happens if a header with `#pragma once` is copied under a different name to another directory, both are included in a `.cpp` file, and we build `Compilation Model — Translation Units, Preprocessing, ODR`?
options: The compiler ignores the duplicate header because the contents are identical.
Both headers are included and parsed, potentially causing redefinition errors.
The linker throws a duplicate symbol error at link time.
The preprocessor automatically merges the duplicate files.
mcqs.explanation: `#pragma once` is file-path or file-inode identity based. If the file is copied to a different path with a different name, `#pragma once` cannot detect it as the same file, so it is included twice, potentially causing redefinition errors.

mcqs.question: If you define a non-inline global variable `int x = 42;` in a header file, and that header is included by two `.cpp` files, what error occurs?
options: A compilation error in both translation units.
A linker error for multiple definitions of symbol `x`.
No error, the variables are merged into a single static storage.
A runtime access violation when `x` is modified.
mcqs.explanation: Each `.cpp` file including the header defines `x` as a global variable with external linkage. When the linker combines the object files, it finds duplicate definitions for symbol `x` and fails to link.

mcqs.question: In C++, what linkage type does a namespace-scope `static` variable or function have?
options: External linkage — visible across all translation units.
Internal linkage — local to the translation unit it is defined in.
No linkage — only visible within the block scope.
Dynamic linkage — resolved at runtime.
mcqs.explanation: The `static` keyword at namespace scope gives the entity internal linkage, meaning its name is only visible and usable within the translation unit where it is defined.

mcqs.question: Why are anonymous namespaces preferred over the `static` keyword for internal linkage in modern C++?
options: Anonymous namespaces are faster at compile time.
`static` cannot be applied to user-defined types (like classes or structs), but anonymous namespaces can.
Anonymous namespaces give external linkage but keep the names hidden.
`static` is deprecated in C++20.
mcqs.explanation: You cannot declare a `static class` or `static struct` at namespace scope to give it internal linkage in C++. Anonymous namespaces solve this by giving internal linkage to all enclosed names, including types, variables, and functions.

mcqs.question: What is the expansion result of the macro `#define MULTIPLY(x, y) x * y` when invoked as `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)`?
options: Compilation error due to invalid operator combination.
mcqs.explanation: Macros perform raw textual substitution. `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)` expands literally to `1 + 2 * 3 + 4`. Due to operator precedence, multiplication runs first (`2 * 3 = 6`), yielding `1 + 6 + 4 = 11`. Always parenthesize macro parameters: `((x) * (y))`.

mcqs.question: What is the static initialization order fiasco in C++?
options: Static local variables are initialized in random order across threads.
The order of initialization of static variables within the same translation unit is undefined.
The order of initialization of non-local static variables in different translation units is undefined.
Compiler optimization silently reorders global constructor calls.
mcqs.explanation: Within a single translation unit, static variables are initialized in order of definition. However, between different translation units, the order of initialization of non-local static variables is undefined, which can cause one static variable to use another uninitialized one.

mcqs.question: Which C++17 feature resolves the header redefinition problem for global constants without violating ODR?
options: `inline` variables.
`constexpr` functions.
Anonymous namespaces.
External template instantiation.
mcqs.explanation: C++17 introduced `inline` variables. If a variable is declared `inline` (e.g. `inline constexpr int MaxValue = 100;`), it can be defined in multiple translation units (such as via header inclusion) and the linker will merge all definitions into a single object.

mcqs.question: How do C++20 modules affect macro visibility compared to `#include` headers?
options: Modules export all macros defined inside them by default.
Macros defined in modules are only visible if the module is imported using `import`.
Modules do not export macros unless explicitly specified, preventing macro pollution.
Modules completely disable macro substitution.
mcqs.explanation: One of the major benefits of C++20 modules is that they do not leak macros. A module file can define macros for internal use, but they will not be exported to the importing file, eliminating name pollution.

subtopics.title: Storage Duration & Linkage
subtopics.explanation:
C++ has four storage durations: automatic (local variables on the stack, destroyed at end of scope), `static` (exist for the entire program lifetime — global/namespace-scope variables, `static` locals, `static` class members), dynamic (allocated via new/malloc, programmer-controlled lifetime), and thread-local (`thread_local` keyword, one instance per thread, C++11).

Linkage determines whether a name can be referred to from other translation units. External linkage means the symbol is visible to the linker across TUs (default for non-const namespace-scope variables and functions). Internal linkage means the symbol is local to its TU — achieved via `static` keyword at namespace scope or anonymous namespaces. No linkage means local variables and function parameters.

Static local variables are initialized the first time control passes through their declaration and persist until program exit. In C++11+, this initialization is guaranteed to be thread-safe (the 'magic statics' guarantee). The `static` keyword on a namespace-scope entity gives it internal linkage, while on a local variable or class member it affects storage duration, not linkage.

### Unforgettable Analogy / Deep Dive
Think of variables in your code like items in a city:
- **Automatic (Stack)** is like a temporary rented scooter. You use it within your local neighborhood (scope) and it is reclaimed immediately when you're done.
- **`Static**` is a historical monument in the town square. It is erected once (initialized) and stays there forever until the city is closed (program exit).
- **Dynamic (Heap)** is a private plot of land that you allocate (`new`) and must explicitly sell (`delete`). If you forget, it stays owned by nobody, causing a land leak (memory leak).
- **Thread-`local**` is like a private passport in each citizen's pocket; each thread gets its own private instance.
- **Internal `Linkage**` is like a local dialect only spoken inside your house (only visible in this translation unit). **External `Linkage**` is like a global language visible across neighborhoods.

questions.question: What are the four storage durations in C++?
questions.answer: Automatic (local stack variables, destroyed at scope exit), static (global/static variables, exist for program lifetime), dynamic (new/delete, programmer-controlled), and thread-local (thread_local, one per thread, C++11+).

questions.question: What is the difference between internal and external linkage?
questions.answer: External linkage means the name is visible across translation units — the linker can resolve references to it from other TUs. Internal linkage means the name is only visible within its TU. Use static or anonymous namespaces for internal linkage.

questions.question: Is static local variable initialization thread-safe?
questions.answer: Yes, since C++11. The standard guarantees that if multiple threads attempt to initialize the same static local concurrently, exactly one will perform the initialization and others will block. This is called 'magic statics'.

subtopics.title: Value Categories — lvalue, prvalue, xvalue, glvalue
subtopics.explanation:
C++11 introduced a refined value category taxonomy to support move semantics. Every expression has two independent properties: does it have identity (can you take its address)? and can it be moved from? This gives the taxonomy: lvalue (has identity, cannot be moved), xvalue (has identity, can be moved — 'eXpiring'), prvalue (no identity, can be moved — 'pure rvalue'). glvalue = lvalue | xvalue (has identity). rvalue = xvalue | prvalue (can be moved).

An lvalue designates a persistent object — a named variable, a dereferenced pointer, a string literal. You can take its address `with &`. A prvalue is a temporary that doesn't have identity — the result of 42, x+y, or a function returning by value. An xvalue is the result of ``std::move`(x)` or a function returning `T&&` — it has identity (refers to an existing object) but is marked as safe to move from.

Understanding value categories is essential for move semantics, perfect forwarding, and understanding when copies vs moves occur. The key insight: `std::move` doesn't move anything — it's just a cast to xvalue (`T&&`), signaling 'you may steal my resources'. The actual move happens when a move constructor/assignment receives this xvalue.

### Unforgettable Analogy / Deep Dive
Think of value categories like items in a shipping warehouse:
- **lvalue (Location Value)** is a labeled storage bin. It has a physical, permanent address in memory (identity) that you can inspect with `&`. You cannot easily move the whole bin, but you can copy items out of it.
- **prvalue (Pure Result Value)** is a physical object flying on a conveyor belt without a label. It has no permanent address (identity), but it is ready to be caught and put into a bin.
- **xvalue (eXpiring Value)** is a labeled storage bin that has a flag saying: 'This bin is about to be demolished, so feel free to steal its contents.' It has an identity, but is marked as safe to move from.
Move semantics simply casts an lvalue (labeled bin) into an xvalue (demolition bin) using `std::move`, allowing the compiler to perform a 'theft by agreement' (move constructor) instead of a slow copy.

questions.question: What are the five value categories in C++11?
questions.answer: lvalue (identity, not movable), xvalue (identity, movable — 'eXpiring'), prvalue (no identity, movable — 'pure rvalue'), glvalue (lvalue or xvalue — has identity), rvalue (xvalue or prvalue — movable).

questions.question: Is a named rvalue reference an lvalue or rvalue?
questions.answer: A named rvalue reference is an lvalue. If you have void foo(std::string&& s), inside foo, 's' is an lvalue because it has a name and identity. You must use std::move(s) to treat it as an rvalue again.

questions.question: What does std::move actually do?
questions.answer: std::move performs an unconditional cast to an xvalue (T&&). It doesn't move anything. It signals to overload resolution that the object can be moved from, so a move constructor or move assignment operator is selected instead of the copy version.

mcqs.question: What happens if you bind a temporary object (prvalue) to a `const T&` reference?
options: The temporary is destroyed at the end of the expression, leaving a dangling reference.
The lifetime of the temporary is extended to match the lifetime of the reference.
The compiler makes a permanent copy of the temporary on the heap.
It is a compilation error.
mcqs.explanation: C++ guarantees that binding a temporary object to a const lvalue reference extends the lifetime of that temporary to match the lifetime of the reference itself, preventing dangling reference bugs.

mcqs.question: What happens if you try to modify a member variable in a `const` member function in `Value Categories — lvalue, prvalue, xvalue, glvalue`?
options: It compiles fine, but triggers a segmentation fault at runtime.
Compilation fails, unless the member variable is marked `mutable`.
It compiles fine, but the changes are discarded when the function exits.
It compiles fine only if the class is not allocated on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: A `const` member function promises not to modify any observable state of the object. Modifying any member variable inside it is a compilation error, unless the member is declared with the `mutable` keyword.

mcqs.question: Can you initialize a `constexpr` variable using the return value of a non-constexpr runtime function?
options: Yes, the compiler will defer evaluation to runtime.
Yes, if the function has no side effects.
No, compilation will fail because a `constexpr` value must be known at compile time.
Yes, but only if compiler optimization is turned on.
mcqs.explanation: `constexpr` variables must be initialized with constant expressions that can be evaluated at compile time. Initializing one with a runtime value results in a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the consequence of calling a `consteval` function with non-constant (runtime) arguments?
options: The function is executed at runtime instead.
The compiler fails to compile the call.
The compiler generates a runtime check that throws an exception if arguments are invalid.
The return value is undefined.
mcqs.explanation: `consteval` (introduced in C++20) specifies an immediate function. Immediate functions MUST be evaluated at compile time. Calling them with runtime values is a compilation error.

mcqs.question: Can a `constinit` variable be modified after initialization during runtime?
options: No, `constinit` variables are implicitly `const`.
Yes, `constinit` only requires compile-time initialization, not runtime immutability.
Yes, but only inside `consteval` functions.
No, modifying it triggers undefined behavior.
mcqs.explanation: `constinit` (C++20) ensures that a variable is initialized at compile time (preventing static initialization order issues), but it does not make the variable constant. To make it constant, you must explicitly combine it with `const`: `constinit const int x = 42;`.

mcqs.question: Is it safe to use `static_cast` to cast a `Base*` to a `Derived*`?
options: Yes, the compiler checks the actual runtime type and returns `nullptr` on failure.
Yes, but it is compile-time checked only. If the pointer is not actually of the Derived type, dereferencing it is UB.
No, it is a compilation error. You must use `dynamic_cast`.
Yes, `static_cast` automatically handles polymorphic conversions safely.
mcqs.explanation: `static_cast` performs compile-time conversions. It does not perform any runtime checks. Casting a base pointer to a derived pointer with `static_cast` is unsafe: if the object is not of the derived type, dereferencing the casted pointer is undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: What does `dynamic_cast` do if it fails to cast a reference type `Base&` to `Derived&`?
options: It returns a null reference.
It throws a `std::bad_cast` exception.
It aborts the program immediately.
It sets the reference to an empty object.
mcqs.explanation: Since there is no such thing as a null reference in C++, `dynamic_cast` cannot return null when casting reference types. Instead, it throws a `std::bad_cast` exception on failure.

mcqs.question: If you cast an `int*` to a `float*` using `reinterpret_cast` and dereference it to read the value, what is the result?
options: It returns the floating-point representation of the integer bits.
It is a compiler error.
It triggers Undefined Behavior due to the strict aliasing rule.
It triggers a hardware trap.
mcqs.explanation: The strict aliasing rule states that you cannot access an object of one type through a pointer of a different type (with exceptions like `char*` or signed/unsigned variants). Violating this using `reinterpret_cast` triggers undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: If both `void print(int)` and `template<typename T> void print(T)` match a call `print(42)` equally well, which one is selected by overload resolution?
options: The template function, because it is more generic.
The non-template function.
The compiler reports an ambiguity error.
The compiler selects one randomly.
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution rules state that if a non-template function and a template specialization match a call equally well, the non-template function is always preferred.

mcqs.question: Does Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) occur if the function call is fully qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)`)?
options: Yes, ADL searches namespaces associated with the type of `x`.
No, ADL is only performed for unqualified function calls.
Yes, but only if `x` is a user-defined type.
No, qualified calls are handled entirely at link time.
mcqs.explanation: Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) only applies to unqualified names (e.g. `foo(x)`). If the call is qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)` or `MyLib::foo(x)`), the compiler uses normal lookup rules and bypasses ADL completely.

subtopics.title: const-correctness — const, constexpr, consteval, constinit
subtopics.explanation:
const means 'this value won't change after initialization' (runtime). `constexpr` (C++11) means 'this can be evaluated at compile time' — a `constexpr` function may run at compile time if given constant arguments, or at runtime otherwise. `consteval` (C++20) means 'this function MUST be evaluated at compile time' — calling it at runtime is an error. `constinit` (C++20) means 'this variable must be initialized at compile time' but can be modified later (prevents the `static` initialization order fiasco).

const-correctness is a design discipline: mark everything const that shouldn't change. const member functions promise not to modify the object's observable state (the this pointer becomes `const T*`). Const references extend the lifetime of temporaries. The mutable keyword allows a member to be modified even in a const context (useful for caches, mutexes).

`constexpr` has been gradually relaxed: C++14 allowed loops and local variables in `constexpr` functions, C++17 added if `constexpr` for compile-time branching, C++20 added `constexpr` `virtual` functions, `constexpr` `std::string`/vector (with transient allocation), and `consteval`/`constinit`.

### Unforgettable Analogy / Deep Dive
Think of constness as levels of lock-down for a treasure chest:
- **`const**` is a read-only padlock. You initialize the variable (at runtime) and lock it. You cannot change it, but it still `requires` checking the lock at runtime.
- **`constexpr**` is pre-calculating the value. Instead of checking the lock, you write the `final` answer directly on the paper before compile-time is over. A `constexpr` function can run at compile time or runtime.
- **`consteval**` is an immediate function. `It **``must**` be pre-calculated before compilation finishes. Calling it with runtime values is a compile error.
- **`constinit**` is setting the starting value at compile time to prevent random initializations (`static` order fiasco), but allowing you to change it later during runtime.

questions.question: What is the difference between const and constexpr?
questions.answer: const means the value won't change after initialization (enforced at runtime). constexpr means the value or function CAN be evaluated at compile time. A constexpr variable is always a compile-time constant; a constexpr function may run at compile or runtime depending on its arguments.

questions.question: What is consteval and when would you use it?

It is a compilation error.

subtopics.title: Casts — static_cast, dynamic_cast, const_cast, reinterpret_cast
subtopics.explanation:
C++ provides four named cast operators, each with a specific purpose and safety level. `static_cast` performs conversions that are checked at compile time — numeric conversions, upcasts, explicit downcasts (unchecked), enum to int, `void*` to typed pointer. `dynamic_cast` performs runtime-checked downcasts using RTTI (`requires` polymorphic base class with at least one `virtual` function) — returns `nullptr` for pointers or throws `std::bad_cast` for references on failure.

`const_cast` adds or removes const/`volatile` qualifiers. It's the only cast that can do this. Modifying a truly const object through `const_cast` is UB. `reinterpret_cast` performs low-level reinterpretation of bit patterns — pointer to int, one pointer type to another. Almost never portable, and most uses violate strict aliasing.

C-style casts ((int)x) try each C++ cast in order: `const_cast`, `static_cast`, `static_cast`+`const_cast`, `reinterpret_cast`, `reinterpret_cast`+`const_cast`. They're dangerous because they silently fall through to `reinterpret_cast` without warning. Always prefer named casts — they make intent explicit and are grep-able.

### Unforgettable Analogy / Deep Dive
Think of C++ casts as different tools in a workshop:
- **`static_cast**` is a standard adapter. You convert integers to floats or base classes to derived classes when you are sure they fit. Checked at compile time.
- **`dynamic_cast**` is a security guard check. It checks the ID (`RTTI`) of a polymorphic pointer at runtime. If the pointer isn't actually a Derived class, it returns `nullptr` or throws. Safest but has runtime cost.
- **`const_cast**` is a key to a display cabinet. It lets you reach inside a const variable to change it (safe only if the original variable wasn't declared const, otherwise it is UB!).
- **`reinterpret_cast**` is looking at a wooden block and claiming it is a block of metal. It forces the compiler to treat the raw bits as another type. Highly dangerous, violates strict aliasing, and is rarely portable.
- **C-style `casts**` are like sledgehammers that force shapes through holes. They try `const_cast`, `static_cast`, and then silently fall back to `reinterpret_cast` without warning.

Use `dynamic_cast` only for runtime-checked polymorphic downcasts
`const_cast` should be rare — typically for interfacing with legacy C APIs

subtopics.title: Overload Resolution Rules and Ambiguity
subtopics.explanation:
When a function call matches multiple overloaded functions, the compiler uses overload resolution to pick the best match. The process: (1) build a candidate set of functions with matching names, (2) filter to viable candidates whose parameters can accept the arguments (with conversions), (3) rank each viable candidate by the conversions required, (4) select the best match or report ambiguity.

Conversion ranking from best to worst: exact match (no conversion) > promotion (char→int, float→double) > standard conversion (int→double, `derived*`→`base*`) > user-defined conversion (constructor or conversion operator) > ellipsis match (...). If two candidates require the same rank of conversion, it's ambiguous.

Key subtleties: const overloads (`f(int&)` vs `f(const int&)`), `template` vs non-`template` (non-`template` preferred if equally good match), and narrowing conversions. Adding overloads can break existing code — an overload that's a better match may be selected instead of a previously used one.

questions.question: What is the order of preference in overload resolution?
questions.answer: Exact match (no conversion needed), then promotion (char/short→int, float→double), then standard conversions (int→double, derived*→base*), then user-defined conversions, then ellipsis (...). Within each rank, more specific matches win.

questions.question: What causes overload ambiguity?
questions.answer: Ambiguity occurs when two or more viable overloads require conversions of equal rank and neither is strictly better. For example, calling f(long) when both f(int) and f(double) exist — long→int and long→double are both standard conversions with no preference.

subtopics.title: Namespaces & ADL (Argument-Dependent Lookup)
subtopics.explanation:
Namespaces prevent name collisions by providing scoped naming. **ADL** (also called Koenig Lookup) is a rule that, for unqualified function calls, the compiler also searches the namespaces of the argument types. This is why `std::cout` << x works without writing `std::`operator<<`` — the compiler finds `operator<<` in namespace std because cout is in std.

**ADL** is essential for operator overloading and generic code. Without it, you'd need to qualify every operator call. However, **ADL** can also cause surprises — a function in an associated namespace might be found when you didn't expect it. The using directive ('using namespace std') imports all names and can cause ambiguity.

Best practices: use using declarations (using `std::vector`) rather than using directives (using namespace std). Never use 'using namespace' in header files. Use `inline` namespaces for API versioning.

examples.title: ADL in Action
examples.explanation: process() is found because w's type is in MyLib, so the compiler searches MyLib.

pitfalls: 'using namespace std' in headers pollutes every includer's namespace

Forgetting that **ADL** doesn't apply to qualified calls (``MyLib::f`()` won't trigger further **ADL**)
tips_to_remember: **ADL** searches the namespaces associated with a function's argument types
Never put 'using namespace' in a header file
Prefer using declarations (using `std::string`) over using directives (using namespace std)
Define `swap()` and operator overloads in the same namespace as your type for **ADL** to find them

questions.question: What is ADL and why does it exist?
questions.answer: Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) automatically searches the namespaces of a function's argument types during unqualified lookup. It exists primarily to make operator overloading work naturally — without it, std::cout << x would require writing std::operator<<(std::cout, x).

questions.question: Why should you never use 'using namespace std' in a header?
questions.answer: Because every file that includes your header would have all of std's names dumped into its scope, causing potential name collisions and ambiguity. It defeats the purpose of namespaces and can silently change the meaning of existing code.

mcqs.question: What is the exact outcome of violating the One Definition Rule (ODR) for an entity across different translation units in C++ when studying `Namespaces & ADL (Argument-Dependent Lookup)`?
options: The compiler will fail to compile with a duplicate definition error.
The linker will always fail to link with a multiple definition error.
The program compiles and links successfully, but triggers Undefined Behavior at runtime.
The program is guaranteed to run correctly if all optimizations are disabled.
mcqs.explanation: ODR violations across different translation units are undefined behavior (UB). Linkers are not required to diagnose them, and they often silently select one definition, leading to random runtime crashes or wrong results.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a translation unit in C++?
options: A single `.cpp` file after preprocessing (with headers expanded).
An individual `.h` header file compiled by itself as a source.
A source file with all its included headers, after macros have been replaced.
A temporary preprocessed file (`.i`) generated by the compiler's preprocessor.
mcqs.explanation: A header file by itself is not a translation unit. A translation unit is a source file (.cpp, .cc) with all its included headers expanded by the preprocessor.

mcqs.question: What happens if a header with `#pragma once` is copied under a different name to another directory, both are included in a `.cpp` file, and we build `Namespaces & ADL (Argument-Dependent Lookup)`?
options: The compiler ignores the duplicate header because the contents are identical.
Both headers are included and parsed, potentially causing redefinition errors.
The linker throws a duplicate symbol error at link time.
The preprocessor automatically merges the duplicate files.
mcqs.explanation: `#pragma once` is file-path or file-inode identity based. If the file is copied to a different path with a different name, `#pragma once` cannot detect it as the same file, so it is included twice, potentially causing redefinition errors.

mcqs.question: If you define a non-inline global variable `int x = 42;` in a header file, and that header is included by two `.cpp` files, what error occurs?
options: A compilation error in both translation units.
A linker error for multiple definitions of symbol `x`.
No error, the variables are merged into a single static storage.
A runtime access violation when `x` is modified.
mcqs.explanation: Each `.cpp` file including the header defines `x` as a global variable with external linkage. When the linker combines the object files, it finds duplicate definitions for symbol `x` and fails to link.

mcqs.question: In C++, what linkage type does a namespace-scope `static` variable or function have?
options: External linkage — visible across all translation units.
Internal linkage — local to the translation unit it is defined in.
No linkage — only visible within the block scope.
Dynamic linkage — resolved at runtime.
mcqs.explanation: The `static` keyword at namespace scope gives the entity internal linkage, meaning its name is only visible and usable within the translation unit where it is defined.

mcqs.question: Why are anonymous namespaces preferred over the `static` keyword for internal linkage in modern C++?
options: Anonymous namespaces are faster at compile time.
`static` cannot be applied to user-defined types (like classes or structs), but anonymous namespaces can.
Anonymous namespaces give external linkage but keep the names hidden.
`static` is deprecated in C++20.
mcqs.explanation: You cannot declare a `static class` or `static struct` at namespace scope to give it internal linkage in C++. Anonymous namespaces solve this by giving internal linkage to all enclosed names, including types, variables, and functions.

mcqs.question: What is the expansion result of the macro `#define MULTIPLY(x, y) x * y` when invoked as `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)`?
options: Compilation error due to invalid operator combination.
mcqs.explanation: Macros perform raw textual substitution. `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)` expands literally to `1 + 2 * 3 + 4`. Due to operator precedence, multiplication runs first (`2 * 3 = 6`), yielding `1 + 6 + 4 = 11`. Always parenthesize macro parameters: `((x) * (y))`.

mcqs.question: What is the static initialization order fiasco in C++?
options: Static local variables are initialized in random order across threads.
The order of initialization of static variables within the same translation unit is undefined.
The order of initialization of non-local static variables in different translation units is undefined.
Compiler optimization silently reorders global constructor calls.
mcqs.explanation: Within a single translation unit, static variables are initialized in order of definition. However, between different translation units, the order of initialization of non-local static variables is undefined, which can cause one static variable to use another uninitialized one.

mcqs.question: Which C++17 feature resolves the header redefinition problem for global constants without violating ODR?
options: `inline` variables.
`constexpr` functions.
Anonymous namespaces.
External template instantiation.
mcqs.explanation: C++17 introduced `inline` variables. If a variable is declared `inline` (e.g. `inline constexpr int MaxValue = 100;`), it can be defined in multiple translation units (such as via header inclusion) and the linker will merge all definitions into a single object.

mcqs.question: How do C++20 modules affect macro visibility compared to `#include` headers?
options: Modules export all macros defined inside them by default.
Macros defined in modules are only visible if the module is imported using `import`.
Modules do not export macros unless explicitly specified, preventing macro pollution.
Modules completely disable macro substitution.
mcqs.explanation: One of the major benefits of C++20 modules is that they do not leak macros. A module file can define macros for internal use, but they will not be exported to the importing file, eliminating name pollution.

subtopics.title: enum vs enum class
subtopics.explanation:
C-style enums (enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }) have several problems: their enumerators leak into the enclosing scope, they implicitly convert to int, and different enums can be compared without warning. enum class (scoped enumerations, C++11) fixes all of these: enumerators are scoped (`Color::Red`), no implicit conversion to int, and you can specify the underlying type.

Always prefer enum class in modern C++. Use `static_cast` when you need integer conversion. You can specify the underlying type for both enum and enum class (enum class Flags : uint8_t).

examples.title: enum vs enum class
examples.explanation: enum class provides type safety and scoping.

pitfalls: Unscoped enums pollute the enclosing namespace with their enumerators
Implicit int conversion of old enums allows comparing unrelated enum types
Forgetting `static_cast` when you need int from enum class
tips_to_remember: Always use enum class unless you need implicit int conversion for legacy interop
Specify underlying type explicitly when you need a specific size (enum class Flags : uint32_t)
Use `to_underlying()` (C++23) or `static_cast` to convert enum class to int

questions.question: What's the difference between enum and enum class?
questions.answer: enum class (C++11) provides scoped enumerators (accessed as Type::Value), no implicit int conversion, and specifiable underlying type. Plain enum leaks names into enclosing scope and implicitly converts to int. Always prefer enum class.

questions.question: How do you convert an enum class to its underlying integer type?
questions.answer: Use static_cast<int>(myEnum) or static_cast<std::underlying_type_t<MyEnum>>(myEnum). C++23 adds std::to_underlying(myEnum) for convenience.

mcqs.question: What happens if you bind a temporary object (prvalue) to a `const T&` reference?
options: The temporary is destroyed at the end of the expression, leaving a dangling reference.
The lifetime of the temporary is extended to match the lifetime of the reference.
The compiler makes a permanent copy of the temporary on the heap.
It is a compilation error.
mcqs.explanation: C++ guarantees that binding a temporary object to a const lvalue reference extends the lifetime of that temporary to match the lifetime of the reference itself, preventing dangling reference bugs.

mcqs.question: What happens if you try to modify a member variable in a `const` member function in `enum vs enum class`?
options: It compiles fine, but triggers a segmentation fault at runtime.
Compilation fails, unless the member variable is marked `mutable`.
It compiles fine, but the changes are discarded when the function exits.
It compiles fine only if the class is not allocated on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: A `const` member function promises not to modify any observable state of the object. Modifying any member variable inside it is a compilation error, unless the member is declared with the `mutable` keyword.

mcqs.question: Can you initialize a `constexpr` variable using the return value of a non-constexpr runtime function?
options: Yes, the compiler will defer evaluation to runtime.
Yes, if the function has no side effects.
No, compilation will fail because a `constexpr` value must be known at compile time.
Yes, but only if compiler optimization is turned on.
mcqs.explanation: `constexpr` variables must be initialized with constant expressions that can be evaluated at compile time. Initializing one with a runtime value results in a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the consequence of calling a `consteval` function with non-constant (runtime) arguments?
options: The function is executed at runtime instead.
The compiler fails to compile the call.
The compiler generates a runtime check that throws an exception if arguments are invalid.
The return value is undefined.
mcqs.explanation: `consteval` (introduced in C++20) specifies an immediate function. Immediate functions MUST be evaluated at compile time. Calling them with runtime values is a compilation error.

mcqs.question: Can a `constinit` variable be modified after initialization during runtime?
options: No, `constinit` variables are implicitly `const`.
Yes, `constinit` only requires compile-time initialization, not runtime immutability.
Yes, but only inside `consteval` functions.
No, modifying it triggers undefined behavior.
mcqs.explanation: `constinit` (C++20) ensures that a variable is initialized at compile time (preventing static initialization order issues), but it does not make the variable constant. To make it constant, you must explicitly combine it with `const`: `constinit const int x = 42;`.

mcqs.question: Is it safe to use `static_cast` to cast a `Base*` to a `Derived*`?
options: Yes, the compiler checks the actual runtime type and returns `nullptr` on failure.
Yes, but it is compile-time checked only. If the pointer is not actually of the Derived type, dereferencing it is UB.
No, it is a compilation error. You must use `dynamic_cast`.
Yes, `static_cast` automatically handles polymorphic conversions safely.
mcqs.explanation: `static_cast` performs compile-time conversions. It does not perform any runtime checks. Casting a base pointer to a derived pointer with `static_cast` is unsafe: if the object is not of the derived type, dereferencing the casted pointer is undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: What does `dynamic_cast` do if it fails to cast a reference type `Base&` to `Derived&`?
options: It returns a null reference.
It throws a `std::bad_cast` exception.
It aborts the program immediately.
It sets the reference to an empty object.
mcqs.explanation: Since there is no such thing as a null reference in C++, `dynamic_cast` cannot return null when casting reference types. Instead, it throws a `std::bad_cast` exception on failure.

mcqs.question: If you cast an `int*` to a `float*` using `reinterpret_cast` and dereference it to read the value, what is the result?
options: It returns the floating-point representation of the integer bits.
It is a compiler error.
It triggers Undefined Behavior due to the strict aliasing rule.
It triggers a hardware trap.
mcqs.explanation: The strict aliasing rule states that you cannot access an object of one type through a pointer of a different type (with exceptions like `char*` or signed/unsigned variants). Violating this using `reinterpret_cast` triggers undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: If both `void print(int)` and `template<typename T> void print(T)` match a call `print(42)` equally well, which one is selected by overload resolution?
options: The template function, because it is more generic.
The non-template function.
The compiler reports an ambiguity error.
The compiler selects one randomly.
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution rules state that if a non-template function and a template specialization match a call equally well, the non-template function is always preferred.

mcqs.question: Does Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) occur if the function call is fully qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)`)?
options: Yes, ADL searches namespaces associated with the type of `x`.
No, ADL is only performed for unqualified function calls.
Yes, but only if `x` is a user-defined type.
No, qualified calls are handled entirely at link time.
mcqs.explanation: Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) only applies to unqualified names (e.g. `foo(x)`). If the call is qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)` or `MyLib::foo(x)`), the compiler uses normal lookup rules and bypasses ADL completely.

subtopics.title: UB vs Unspecified vs Implementation-Defined Behavior
subtopics.explanation:
Undefined Behavior (UB) means the standard imposes NO requirements — anything can happen (crash, wrong result, nasal demons, time travel). Examples: signed integer overflow, null pointer dereference, use-after-free, data races, out-of-bounds access. Compilers assume UB never happens and optimize accordingly.

Implementation-defined behavior has a specific result that the compiler must document. Examples: `sizeof(int)`, right-shift of negative integers, char being signed or unsigned. Your code may depend on it, but it's portable only if you check.

Unspecified behavior means the standard provides a set of valid options, and the compiler may choose any without documenting which. Examples: order of evaluation of function arguments, order of evaluation of operands (mostly fixed in C++17).

examples.title: The Three Kinds
examples.explanation: Understanding these distinctions is critical for writing portable, correct code.

pitfalls: Assuming signed overflow wraps around (it's UB, not unspecified)
Relying on evaluation order of function arguments
Assuming int is always 32 bits (it's implementation-defined)
Compilers optimize assuming UB never happens — this can remove 'safety' checks
tips_to_remember: If the standard says UB, your program has no meaning — any result is conforming
Compilers exploit UB for optimization: 'this path has UB → this path is unreachable → optimize it away'
Use sanitizers (UBSan, ASan) to catch UB at runtime
When in doubt, check the standard or cppreference.com

questions.question: What is undefined behavior and why is it dangerous?
questions.answer: UB means the C++ standard imposes zero requirements on program behavior. Compilers assume UB never occurs and may optimize code in unexpected ways based on that assumption. This means UB can cause bugs far from the actual problematic code.

questions.question: Give 5 examples of undefined behavior.
questions.answer: 1) Signed integer overflow, 2) Dereferencing null/dangling pointers, 3) Accessing array out of bounds, 4) Data races (unsynchronized concurrent access), 5) Using an object after its lifetime ends (use-after-free). All have no defined behavior — any outcome is valid.

subtopics.title: Preprocessor Macros vs Modern Replacements
subtopics.explanation:
The C preprocessor is a text substitution engine that runs before the compiler. Macros (`#define`) have many problems: no type safety, no scope, hard to debug, can have surprising expansions due to operator precedence. Modern C++ provides superior alternatives: templates (generic code), `constexpr` (compile-time constants and computation), `inline` functions (avoid function call overhead), and enum class (named constants).

Legitimate remaining uses of macros: include guards, conditional compilation (`#ifdef`), platform-specific code, and a few corner cases like __LINE__/__FILE__ for logging. Avoid function-like macros entirely — use templates or `inline` functions instead.

examples.title: Macro vs Modern Alternatives
examples.explanation: Macros have no type safety and can double-evaluate arguments. constexpr/templates are always better.

pitfalls: Macro arguments evaluated multiple times (double evaluation bug)
Macros don't respect scope — they pollute the global namespace
Macros can't be debugged — the debugger sees expanded code
Macro names can conflict with other identifiers (e.g., `#define max` clashes with `std::max`)
tips_to_remember: Use `constexpr` variables instead of `#define constants`
Use `inline` functions or templates instead of function-like macros
Use enum class for groups of related constants
Only use macros for include guards, conditional compilation, and __LINE__/__FILE__

questions.question: Why are macros discouraged in modern C++?
questions.answer: Macros are text substitutions with no type safety, no scope, no debugging support, and can cause bugs through double evaluation and name collisions. Every macro use case has a safer modern alternative: constexpr for constants, templates/inline for generic code, enum class for enumerations.

questions.question: What macro uses are still legitimate in modern C++?
questions.answer: Include guards (#ifndef/#pragma once), conditional compilation (#ifdef for platform-specific code), stringification (#) and token pasting (##) for code generation, and __LINE__/__FILE__/__func__ for logging/diagnostics. Everything else should use constexpr, templates, or inline.

mcqs.question: What is the exact outcome of violating the One Definition Rule (ODR) for an entity across different translation units in C++ when studying `Preprocessor Macros vs Modern Replacements`?
options: The compiler will fail to compile with a duplicate definition error.
The linker will always fail to link with a multiple definition error.
The program compiles and links successfully, but triggers Undefined Behavior at runtime.
The program is guaranteed to run correctly if all optimizations are disabled.
mcqs.explanation: ODR violations across different translation units are undefined behavior (UB). Linkers are not required to diagnose them, and they often silently select one definition, leading to random runtime crashes or wrong results.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is NOT a translation unit in C++?
options: A single `.cpp` file after preprocessing (with headers expanded).
An individual `.h` header file compiled by itself as a source.
A source file with all its included headers, after macros have been replaced.
A temporary preprocessed file (`.i`) generated by the compiler's preprocessor.
mcqs.explanation: A header file by itself is not a translation unit. A translation unit is a source file (.cpp, .cc) with all its included headers expanded by the preprocessor.

mcqs.question: What happens if a header with `#pragma once` is copied under a different name to another directory, both are included in a `.cpp` file, and we build `Preprocessor Macros vs Modern Replacements`?
options: The compiler ignores the duplicate header because the contents are identical.
Both headers are included and parsed, potentially causing redefinition errors.
The linker throws a duplicate symbol error at link time.
The preprocessor automatically merges the duplicate files.
mcqs.explanation: `#pragma once` is file-path or file-inode identity based. If the file is copied to a different path with a different name, `#pragma once` cannot detect it as the same file, so it is included twice, potentially causing redefinition errors.

mcqs.question: If you define a non-inline global variable `int x = 42;` in a header file, and that header is included by two `.cpp` files, what error occurs?
options: A compilation error in both translation units.
A linker error for multiple definitions of symbol `x`.
No error, the variables are merged into a single static storage.
A runtime access violation when `x` is modified.
mcqs.explanation: Each `.cpp` file including the header defines `x` as a global variable with external linkage. When the linker combines the object files, it finds duplicate definitions for symbol `x` and fails to link.

mcqs.question: In C++, what linkage type does a namespace-scope `static` variable or function have?
options: External linkage — visible across all translation units.
Internal linkage — local to the translation unit it is defined in.
No linkage — only visible within the block scope.
Dynamic linkage — resolved at runtime.
mcqs.explanation: The `static` keyword at namespace scope gives the entity internal linkage, meaning its name is only visible and usable within the translation unit where it is defined.

mcqs.question: Why are anonymous namespaces preferred over the `static` keyword for internal linkage in modern C++?
options: Anonymous namespaces are faster at compile time.
`static` cannot be applied to user-defined types (like classes or structs), but anonymous namespaces can.
Anonymous namespaces give external linkage but keep the names hidden.
`static` is deprecated in C++20.
mcqs.explanation: You cannot declare a `static class` or `static struct` at namespace scope to give it internal linkage in C++. Anonymous namespaces solve this by giving internal linkage to all enclosed names, including types, variables, and functions.

mcqs.question: What is the expansion result of the macro `#define MULTIPLY(x, y) x * y` when invoked as `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)`?
options: Compilation error due to invalid operator combination.
mcqs.explanation: Macros perform raw textual substitution. `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)` expands literally to `1 + 2 * 3 + 4`. Due to operator precedence, multiplication runs first (`2 * 3 = 6`), yielding `1 + 6 + 4 = 11`. Always parenthesize macro parameters: `((x) * (y))`.

mcqs.question: What is the static initialization order fiasco in C++?
options: Static local variables are initialized in random order across threads.
The order of initialization of static variables within the same translation unit is undefined.
The order of initialization of non-local static variables in different translation units is undefined.
Compiler optimization silently reorders global constructor calls.
mcqs.explanation: Within a single translation unit, static variables are initialized in order of definition. However, between different translation units, the order of initialization of non-local static variables is undefined, which can cause one static variable to use another uninitialized one.

mcqs.question: Which C++17 feature resolves the header redefinition problem for global constants without violating ODR?
options: `inline` variables.
`constexpr` functions.
Anonymous namespaces.
External template instantiation.
mcqs.explanation: C++17 introduced `inline` variables. If a variable is declared `inline` (e.g. `inline constexpr int MaxValue = 100;`), it can be defined in multiple translation units (such as via header inclusion) and the linker will merge all definitions into a single object.

mcqs.question: How do C++20 modules affect macro visibility compared to `#include` headers?
options: Modules export all macros defined inside them by default.
Macros defined in modules are only visible if the module is imported using `import`.
Modules do not export macros unless explicitly specified, preventing macro pollution.
Modules completely disable macro substitution.
mcqs.explanation: One of the major benefits of C++20 modules is that they do not leak macros. A module file can define macros for internal use, but they will not be exported to the importing file, eliminating name pollution.

subtopics.title: Raw Pointers & Pointer Arithmetic
subtopics.explanation:
A pointer holds the memory address of an object. Pointer arithmetic moves in units of the pointed-to type's size: p+1 advances by `sizeof(*p)` bytes. This is fundamental to array traversal and low-level memory manipulation.

Pointer arithmetic is only defined within arrays (including one-past-the-end). Arithmetic on unrelated pointers is UB. Subtraction of two pointers to elements of the same array yields ptrdiff_t (the number of elements between them).

Modern C++ rarely needs raw pointer arithmetic — prefer iterators, spans, or algorithms. Raw pointers are still used for non-owning observation and interfacing with C APIs.

examples.title: Pointer Arithmetic
examples.explanation: Pointer arithmetic works in units of the element type's size.

examples.title: Array Access is Pointer Arithmetic
examples.explanation: arr[i] is syntactic sugar for *(arr+i), which is why i[arr] works (but is terrible style).

pitfalls: Pointer arithmetic past array bounds (other than one-past-end) is UB
Dereferencing one-past-the-end pointer is UB (you can form it, not dereference it)
Subtracting pointers to different arrays is UB
Forgetting that p++ advances by `sizeof(*p)` bytes, not 1 byte
tips_to_remember: Pointer arithmetic is only valid within the same array
arr[i] is `exactly *`(arr + i) — understand this equivalence
Use `std::span` or iterators instead of raw pointer arithmetic in modern code
`nullptr` dereference is UB — always check before dereferencing

questions.question: What is pointer arithmetic and how does it work?
questions.answer: Pointer arithmetic moves a pointer by multiples of the pointed-to type's size. p+n advances p by n*sizeof(*p) bytes. It's only defined for pointers within the same array (or one past the end). Subtraction of two pointers in the same array gives the element count between them.

questions.question: Is pointer arithmetic on unrelated pointers defined?
questions.answer: No. Comparing or subtracting pointers that don't point into the same array (or one past its end) is undefined behavior. The result is meaningless.

mcqs.question: What happens when you pass an array `int arr[10]` to a function declared as `void process(int arr[])`?
options: The array is passed by value, making a copy of all 10 integers.
It decays to a raw pointer `int*`, and its size information is lost.
The compiler verifies the size is exactly 10 and throws a warning if not.
It is passed as a safe reference to the array.
mcqs.explanation: Arrays passed to functions decay to pointers. Inside `process`, `arr` is a raw pointer (`int*`), and `sizeof(arr)` returns the pointer size (e.g. 8 bytes), not the array size.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a compiler error for `std::unique_ptr`?
options: Moving it using `std::move`.
Attempting to copy it via copy assignment or copy constructor.
Resetting it using `.reset()`.
Releasing ownership with `.release()`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::unique_ptr` represents exclusive ownership. To prevent duplicate owners, copying is disabled (deleted copy constructor/assignment), causing a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the outcome of a circular dependency where two objects contain `std::shared_ptr` pointing to each other?
options: The compiler reports a cyclic template dependency error.
The reference counts will never drop to zero, leaking both objects.
The destructors are called normally due to automatic cycle detection.
The program crashes with a stack overflow on deletion.
mcqs.explanation: Because each object holds a `std::shared_ptr` to the other, their reference counts remain at least 1, even after all external pointers are destroyed, leaking the memory.

mcqs.question: How do you access the managed object of a `std::weak_ptr`?
options: Dereference it directly using `*` or `->`.
You must call `.lock()` to obtain a `std::shared_ptr` first.
Call `.get()` to retrieve the raw pointer.
It is not possible to access the object once it is in a weak pointer.
mcqs.explanation: `std::weak_ptr` does not provide direct access. You must call `.lock()` which returns a `std::shared_ptr`. If the managed object has already been destroyed, the returned shared pointer will be empty.

mcqs.question: What is the primary benefit of using `std::make_shared` instead of `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
options: It makes the shared pointer thread-safe.
It performs a single memory allocation for both the control block and the object, improving performance and cache locality.
It allows using custom delete functions.
It prevents compile-time template instantiation overhead.
mcqs.explanation: `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)` allocates the object first, then allocates the control block. `std::make_shared` allocates a single block of memory big enough to hold both, reducing heap allocation overhead.

mcqs.question: How does a custom deleter function pointer affect the size of a `std::unique_ptr`?
options: It does not affect the size; it remains 8 bytes.
It increases the size of the pointer (typically to 16 bytes) because it must store the function pointer.
It causes the unique_ptr to allocate memory on the heap.
It is a compile-time construct and does not exist at runtime.
mcqs.explanation: If a custom deleter is a function pointer, the unique_ptr must store it, increasing its size. Using a stateless functor (like a lambda with no captures) avoids this size overhead.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of placement `new` in C++?
options: It automatically finds the best place in the heap to allocate memory.
It constructs an object on a pre-allocated raw memory buffer without allocating new heap memory.
It moves an object to another thread's stack space.
It optimizes memory alignment dynamically.
mcqs.explanation: Placement `new` (e.g. `new (buffer) MyClass()`) constructs an object at a specific, pre-allocated memory address, avoiding heap allocation costs.

mcqs.question: How must you destroy an object constructed via placement `new`?
options: Call `delete ptr;`.
Explicitly call the object's destructor (`ptr->~T()`) and then manually manage the buffer's memory.
Let it go out of scope; the stack automatically deletes it.
Call `free(ptr);`.
mcqs.explanation: Because placement `new` did not allocate memory from the global heap, calling `delete` is undefined behavior. You must explicitly invoke the destructor and then clean up the raw buffer.

mcqs.question: What is the undefined behavior hazard in the code `int* p = new int[10]; delete p;`?
options: Using the wrong delete operator (`delete` instead of `delete[]`) is Undefined Behavior.
There is no hazard; `delete` automatically knows it is an array.
It is a compiler error and won't compile.
It causes a stack overflow.
mcqs.explanation: Memory allocated with `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`. Using plain `delete` on an array pointer is undefined behavior, often causing heap corruption or failing to call destructors for elements 1 to 9.

mcqs.question: What is the risk of returning a local variable by reference `const int&` from a function?
options: It copies the variable unnecessarily.
The local variable is destroyed at function exit, leaving a dangling reference, and accessing it is UB.
It compiles only if the variable is marked `static`.
It causes a memory leak on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: Local variables have automatic storage duration (stack-allocated) and are destroyed when the function returns. Accessing a reference to a destroyed local variable is undefined behavior.

subtopics.title: References vs Pointers — Binding Rules
subtopics.explanation:
A reference is an alias for an existing object. Unlike pointers, references must be initialized at declaration, cannot be rebound to a different object, and cannot be null. Syntactically, you use a reference like the original object (`no *` dereference needed).

There are three kinds of references: lvalue references (`T&`), const lvalue references (`const T&`), and rvalue references (`T&&`, C++11). A const lvalue reference can bind to temporaries and extends their lifetime (until the reference goes out of scope). An rvalue reference can also bind to temporaries.

Prefer references over pointers when: the target is guaranteed to exist (non-null), you don't need to reseat, and you want cleaner syntax. Use pointers when: nullability is needed, reseating is needed, or you need pointer arithmetic.

examples.title: References vs Pointers
examples.explanation: References are safer aliases — no null, no rebinding, no dereferencing syntax.

pitfalls: Returning a reference to a local variable — creates a dangling reference (UB)
const reference lifetime extension doesn't work through function returns
References can't be stored in containers (use `std::reference_wrapper`)
A reference to a temporary only extends lifetime for const lvalue and rvalue references
tips_to_remember: References can't be null — use when the target must exist
Prefer `const T&` for function parameters to avoid copies
Use `T&&` for move semantics and perfect forwarding
A reference is NOT a pointer under the hood (conceptually) — though compilers may implement it as one

questions.question: What are the key differences between references and pointers?
questions.answer: References: must be initialized, cannot be null, cannot be rebound, no dereference syntax needed. Pointers: can be null, can be reseated, require * to dereference, support arithmetic. References are generally safer and preferred when possible.

questions.question: Can a reference be null?
questions.answer: No, by specification. A reference must always refer to a valid object. Creating a reference to null (e.g., int& r = *static_cast<int*>(nullptr)) is undefined behavior at the point of creation, even before you use it.

mcqs.question: What happens when you pass an array `int arr[10]` to a function declared as `void process(int arr[])`?
options: The array is passed by value, making a copy of all 10 integers.
It decays to a raw pointer `int*`, and its size information is lost.
The compiler verifies the size is exactly 10 and throws a warning if not.
It is passed as a safe reference to the array.
mcqs.explanation: Arrays passed to functions decay to pointers. Inside `process`, `arr` is a raw pointer (`int*`), and `sizeof(arr)` returns the pointer size (e.g. 8 bytes), not the array size.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a compiler error for `std::unique_ptr`?
options: Moving it using `std::move`.
Attempting to copy it via copy assignment or copy constructor.
Resetting it using `.reset()`.
Releasing ownership with `.release()`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::unique_ptr` represents exclusive ownership. To prevent duplicate owners, copying is disabled (deleted copy constructor/assignment), causing a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the outcome of a circular dependency where two objects contain `std::shared_ptr` pointing to each other?
options: The compiler reports a cyclic template dependency error.
The reference counts will never drop to zero, leaking both objects.
The destructors are called normally due to automatic cycle detection.
The program crashes with a stack overflow on deletion.
mcqs.explanation: Because each object holds a `std::shared_ptr` to the other, their reference counts remain at least 1, even after all external pointers are destroyed, leaking the memory.

mcqs.question: How do you access the managed object of a `std::weak_ptr`?
options: Dereference it directly using `*` or `->`.
You must call `.lock()` to obtain a `std::shared_ptr` first.
Call `.get()` to retrieve the raw pointer.
It is not possible to access the object once it is in a weak pointer.
mcqs.explanation: `std::weak_ptr` does not provide direct access. You must call `.lock()` which returns a `std::shared_ptr`. If the managed object has already been destroyed, the returned shared pointer will be empty.

mcqs.question: What is the primary benefit of using `std::make_shared` instead of `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
options: It makes the shared pointer thread-safe.
It performs a single memory allocation for both the control block and the object, improving performance and cache locality.
It allows using custom delete functions.
It prevents compile-time template instantiation overhead.
mcqs.explanation: `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)` allocates the object first, then allocates the control block. `std::make_shared` allocates a single block of memory big enough to hold both, reducing heap allocation overhead.

mcqs.question: How does a custom deleter function pointer affect the size of a `std::unique_ptr`?
options: It does not affect the size; it remains 8 bytes.
It increases the size of the pointer (typically to 16 bytes) because it must store the function pointer.
It causes the unique_ptr to allocate memory on the heap.
It is a compile-time construct and does not exist at runtime.
mcqs.explanation: If a custom deleter is a function pointer, the unique_ptr must store it, increasing its size. Using a stateless functor (like a lambda with no captures) avoids this size overhead.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of placement `new` in C++?
options: It automatically finds the best place in the heap to allocate memory.
It constructs an object on a pre-allocated raw memory buffer without allocating new heap memory.
It moves an object to another thread's stack space.
It optimizes memory alignment dynamically.
mcqs.explanation: Placement `new` (e.g. `new (buffer) MyClass()`) constructs an object at a specific, pre-allocated memory address, avoiding heap allocation costs.

mcqs.question: How must you destroy an object constructed via placement `new`?
options: Call `delete ptr;`.
Explicitly call the object's destructor (`ptr->~T()`) and then manually manage the buffer's memory.
Let it go out of scope; the stack automatically deletes it.
Call `free(ptr);`.
mcqs.explanation: Because placement `new` did not allocate memory from the global heap, calling `delete` is undefined behavior. You must explicitly invoke the destructor and then clean up the raw buffer.

mcqs.question: What is the undefined behavior hazard in the code `int* p = new int[10]; delete p;`?
options: Using the wrong delete operator (`delete` instead of `delete[]`) is Undefined Behavior.
There is no hazard; `delete` automatically knows it is an array.
It is a compiler error and won't compile.
It causes a stack overflow.
mcqs.explanation: Memory allocated with `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`. Using plain `delete` on an array pointer is undefined behavior, often causing heap corruption or failing to call destructors for elements 1 to 9.

mcqs.question: What is the risk of returning a local variable by reference `const int&` from a function?
options: It copies the variable unnecessarily.
The local variable is destroyed at function exit, leaving a dangling reference, and accessing it is UB.
It compiles only if the variable is marked `static`.
It causes a memory leak on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: Local variables have automatic storage duration (stack-allocated) and are destroyed when the function returns. Accessing a reference to a destroyed local variable is undefined behavior.

subtopics.title: Function Pointers & Pointer-to-Member
subtopics.explanation:
A function pointer stores the address of a function. The syntax is: ReturnType (*name)(ParamTypes). You can call through it like a regular function. C++ also has pointer-to-member-function and pointer-to-data-member, which are fundamentally different — they require an object to invoke (using .* or ->*).

Pointer-to-member-function has type: ReturnType (ClassName::*)(ParamTypes). It cannot be implicitly converted to a regular function pointer because it needs a 'this' pointer. Member function pointers may be larger than regular pointers (to handle `virtual` functions and multiple inheritance).

In modern C++, prefer lambdas, `std::function`, or templates over raw function pointers. They're more flexible and can capture state.

examples.title: Function Pointers
examples.explanation: Function pointers let you select functions at runtime — the basis for callbacks.

examples.title: Pointer-to-Member
examples.explanation: Member pointers need an object instance — accessed with .* or ->*.

pitfalls: Member function pointers are NOT regular function pointers — can't interchange them
Member function pointers may be larger than `sizeof(void*)` due to `virtual` dispatch info
Calling a `virtual` function through a pointer-to-member correctly dispatches virtually
C-style function pointers can't capture state — use lambdas or `std::function` instead
tips_to_remember: Use using or typedef to make function pointer types readable
Prefer lambdas and `std::function` over raw function pointers in modern C++
Pointer-to-member `requires` .* or ->* syntax — can't call without an object
`std::invoke` (C++17) uniformly calls functions, member functions, and member pointers

questions.question: How do member function pointers differ from regular function pointers?
questions.answer: Member function pointers need an object to call through (using .* or ->*), have a different type signature (RetType (Class::*)(Params)), may be larger in size, and cannot be converted to regular function pointers.

questions.question: What is std::invoke and why is it useful?
questions.answer: std::invoke (C++17) provides a uniform way to call any callable: regular functions, function pointers, member function pointers, member data pointers, lambdas, and functors — all with the same syntax. It simplifies generic code.
