subtopics.title: Sanitizers — ASan, UBSan, TSan, MSan
subtopics.explanation:
AddressSanitizer (ASan): detects buffer overflows, use-after-free, double-free, memory leaks. ~2x slowdown. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan): detects signed overflow, null dereference, alignment violations, shift past bit-width. Minimal overhead. ThreadSanitizer (TSan): detects data races. ~5-15x slowdown. MemorySanitizer (MSan): detects use of uninitialized memory. ~3x slowdown.

Enable with compiler flags: -fsanitize=address, -fsanitize=undefined, etc. Run your test suite with sanitizers regularly.

examples.title: Using Sanitizers
examples.explanation: Compile with -fsanitize=X to enable. Run normally — sanitizer reports errors at runtime.

pitfalls: Not running sanitizers regularly in CI — bugs slip through
ASan and TSan can't be used simultaneously
MSan `requires` the entire program (including libraries) to be instrumented
tips_to_remember: Run ASan and UBSan in CI on every commit
TSan finds data races that are otherwise nearly impossible to reproduce
Use -fno-omit-frame-pointer with sanitizers for better stack traces
ASan + UBSan can be combined: -fsanitize=address,undefined

questions.question: What are the four main sanitizers?
questions.answer: ASan (memory errors: overflow, use-after-free, leaks), UBSan (undefined behavior: overflow, alignment, null deref), TSan (data races), MSan (uninitialized reads). All are compile-time instrumentation.

questions.question: Can you combine sanitizers?
questions.answer: ASan + UBSan: yes. ASan + TSan: no (incompatible). MSan + ASan: no. TSan + UBSan: yes. Typical CI setup: one build with ASan+UBSan, another with TSan.

mcqs.question: What happens if you bind a temporary object (prvalue) to a `const T&` reference?
options: The temporary is destroyed at the end of the expression, leaving a dangling reference.
The lifetime of the temporary is extended to match the lifetime of the reference.
The compiler makes a permanent copy of the temporary on the heap.
It is a compilation error.
mcqs.explanation: C++ guarantees that binding a temporary object to a const lvalue reference extends the lifetime of that temporary to match the lifetime of the reference itself, preventing dangling reference bugs.

mcqs.question: What happens if you try to modify a member variable in a `const` member function in `Sanitizers — ASan, UBSan, TSan, MSan`?
options: It compiles fine, but triggers a segmentation fault at runtime.
Compilation fails, unless the member variable is marked `mutable`.
It compiles fine, but the changes are discarded when the function exits.
It compiles fine only if the class is not allocated on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: A `const` member function promises not to modify any observable state of the object. Modifying any member variable inside it is a compilation error, unless the member is declared with the `mutable` keyword.

mcqs.question: Can you initialize a `constexpr` variable using the return value of a non-constexpr runtime function?
options: Yes, the compiler will defer evaluation to runtime.
Yes, if the function has no side effects.
No, compilation will fail because a `constexpr` value must be known at compile time.
Yes, but only if compiler optimization is turned on.
mcqs.explanation: `constexpr` variables must be initialized with constant expressions that can be evaluated at compile time. Initializing one with a runtime value results in a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the consequence of calling a `consteval` function with non-constant (runtime) arguments?
options: The function is executed at runtime instead.
The compiler fails to compile the call.
The compiler generates a runtime check that throws an exception if arguments are invalid.
The return value is undefined.
mcqs.explanation: `consteval` (introduced in C++20) specifies an immediate function. Immediate functions MUST be evaluated at compile time. Calling them with runtime values is a compilation error.

mcqs.question: Can a `constinit` variable be modified after initialization during runtime?
options: No, `constinit` variables are implicitly `const`.
Yes, `constinit` only requires compile-time initialization, not runtime immutability.
Yes, but only inside `consteval` functions.
No, modifying it triggers undefined behavior.
mcqs.explanation: `constinit` (C++20) ensures that a variable is initialized at compile time (preventing static initialization order issues), but it does not make the variable constant. To make it constant, you must explicitly combine it with `const`: `constinit const int x = 42;`.

mcqs.question: Is it safe to use `static_cast` to cast a `Base*` to a `Derived*`?
options: Yes, the compiler checks the actual runtime type and returns `nullptr` on failure.
Yes, but it is compile-time checked only. If the pointer is not actually of the Derived type, dereferencing it is UB.
No, it is a compilation error. You must use `dynamic_cast`.
Yes, `static_cast` automatically handles polymorphic conversions safely.
mcqs.explanation: `static_cast` performs compile-time conversions. It does not perform any runtime checks. Casting a base pointer to a derived pointer with `static_cast` is unsafe: if the object is not of the derived type, dereferencing the casted pointer is undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: What does `dynamic_cast` do if it fails to cast a reference type `Base&` to `Derived&`?
options: It returns a null reference.
It throws a `std::bad_cast` exception.
It aborts the program immediately.
It sets the reference to an empty object.
mcqs.explanation: Since there is no such thing as a null reference in C++, `dynamic_cast` cannot return null when casting reference types. Instead, it throws a `std::bad_cast` exception on failure.

mcqs.question: If you cast an `int*` to a `float*` using `reinterpret_cast` and dereference it to read the value, what is the result?
options: It returns the floating-point representation of the integer bits.
It is a compiler error.
It triggers Undefined Behavior due to the strict aliasing rule.
It triggers a hardware trap.
mcqs.explanation: The strict aliasing rule states that you cannot access an object of one type through a pointer of a different type (with exceptions like `char*` or signed/unsigned variants). Violating this using `reinterpret_cast` triggers undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: If both `void print(int)` and `template<typename T> void print(T)` match a call `print(42)` equally well, which one is selected by overload resolution?
options: The template function, because it is more generic.
The non-template function.
The compiler reports an ambiguity error.
The compiler selects one randomly.
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution rules state that if a non-template function and a template specialization match a call equally well, the non-template function is always preferred.

mcqs.question: Does Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) occur if the function call is fully qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)`)?
options: Yes, ADL searches namespaces associated with the type of `x`.
No, ADL is only performed for unqualified function calls.
Yes, but only if `x` is a user-defined type.
No, qualified calls are handled entirely at link time.
mcqs.explanation: Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) only applies to unqualified names (e.g. `foo(x)`). If the call is qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)` or `MyLib::foo(x)`), the compiler uses normal lookup rules and bypasses ADL completely.

subtopics.title: Common UB Traps
subtopics.explanation:
Signed integer overflow (INT_MAX + 1), strict aliasing violations (casting `float*` to `int*` and dereferencing), uninitialized reads, null pointer dereference, shift by negative or >= bit-width, infinite loops without side effects (optimizer may remove them), modifying a const object through `const_cast`.

Compilers assume UB never happens and optimize accordingly. This means UB can cause code to be removed, reordered, or produce impossible results.

examples.title: UB Examples
examples.explanation: These are the most common UB traps. Use UBSan to detect them at runtime.

pitfalls: Assuming signed overflow wraps (it doesn't in C++ — use unsigned for wrap-around)
Type punning through pointer casts — use memcpy
Uninitialized local variables — always initialize
Shift operators with negative or too-large shift amounts
tips_to_remember: Use -Werror -Wall -Wextra and sanitizers to catch UB
unsigned arithmetic wraps (defined). signed arithmetic overflows (UB).
Always initialize variables. Use {} for zero-initialization.
memcpy is the safe way to type-pun. `reinterpret_cast` on values is UB.

questions.question: Why is signed integer overflow UB?
questions.answer: The standard doesn't define wrap-around behavior for signed integers (unlike unsigned). Compilers exploit this: if x > 0, the optimizer assumes x+1 > 0 too (since overflow 'can't happen'). This enables optimizations like loop bound simplification.

questions.question: What is strict aliasing and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The rule that an object can only be accessed through a pointer of its actual type (or char/byte). Violating it is UB. The compiler assumes different-typed pointers don't alias, enabling register optimization. Breaking it causes bugs at -O2 that don't appear at -O0.

mcqs.question: What happens if you bind a temporary object (prvalue) to a `const T&` reference?
options: The temporary is destroyed at the end of the expression, leaving a dangling reference.
The lifetime of the temporary is extended to match the lifetime of the reference.
The compiler makes a permanent copy of the temporary on the heap.
It is a compilation error.
mcqs.explanation: C++ guarantees that binding a temporary object to a const lvalue reference extends the lifetime of that temporary to match the lifetime of the reference itself, preventing dangling reference bugs.

mcqs.question: What happens if you try to modify a member variable in a `const` member function in `Common UB Traps`?
options: It compiles fine, but triggers a segmentation fault at runtime.
Compilation fails, unless the member variable is marked `mutable`.
It compiles fine, but the changes are discarded when the function exits.
It compiles fine only if the class is not allocated on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: A `const` member function promises not to modify any observable state of the object. Modifying any member variable inside it is a compilation error, unless the member is declared with the `mutable` keyword.

mcqs.question: Can you initialize a `constexpr` variable using the return value of a non-constexpr runtime function?
options: Yes, the compiler will defer evaluation to runtime.
Yes, if the function has no side effects.
No, compilation will fail because a `constexpr` value must be known at compile time.
Yes, but only if compiler optimization is turned on.
mcqs.explanation: `constexpr` variables must be initialized with constant expressions that can be evaluated at compile time. Initializing one with a runtime value results in a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the consequence of calling a `consteval` function with non-constant (runtime) arguments?
options: The function is executed at runtime instead.
The compiler fails to compile the call.
The compiler generates a runtime check that throws an exception if arguments are invalid.
The return value is undefined.
mcqs.explanation: `consteval` (introduced in C++20) specifies an immediate function. Immediate functions MUST be evaluated at compile time. Calling them with runtime values is a compilation error.

mcqs.question: Can a `constinit` variable be modified after initialization during runtime?
options: No, `constinit` variables are implicitly `const`.
Yes, `constinit` only requires compile-time initialization, not runtime immutability.
Yes, but only inside `consteval` functions.
No, modifying it triggers undefined behavior.
mcqs.explanation: `constinit` (C++20) ensures that a variable is initialized at compile time (preventing static initialization order issues), but it does not make the variable constant. To make it constant, you must explicitly combine it with `const`: `constinit const int x = 42;`.

mcqs.question: Is it safe to use `static_cast` to cast a `Base*` to a `Derived*`?
options: Yes, the compiler checks the actual runtime type and returns `nullptr` on failure.
Yes, but it is compile-time checked only. If the pointer is not actually of the Derived type, dereferencing it is UB.
No, it is a compilation error. You must use `dynamic_cast`.
Yes, `static_cast` automatically handles polymorphic conversions safely.
mcqs.explanation: `static_cast` performs compile-time conversions. It does not perform any runtime checks. Casting a base pointer to a derived pointer with `static_cast` is unsafe: if the object is not of the derived type, dereferencing the casted pointer is undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: What does `dynamic_cast` do if it fails to cast a reference type `Base&` to `Derived&`?
options: It returns a null reference.
It throws a `std::bad_cast` exception.
It aborts the program immediately.
It sets the reference to an empty object.
mcqs.explanation: Since there is no such thing as a null reference in C++, `dynamic_cast` cannot return null when casting reference types. Instead, it throws a `std::bad_cast` exception on failure.

mcqs.question: If you cast an `int*` to a `float*` using `reinterpret_cast` and dereference it to read the value, what is the result?
options: It returns the floating-point representation of the integer bits.
It is a compiler error.
It triggers Undefined Behavior due to the strict aliasing rule.
It triggers a hardware trap.
mcqs.explanation: The strict aliasing rule states that you cannot access an object of one type through a pointer of a different type (with exceptions like `char*` or signed/unsigned variants). Violating this using `reinterpret_cast` triggers undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: If both `void print(int)` and `template<typename T> void print(T)` match a call `print(42)` equally well, which one is selected by overload resolution?
options: The template function, because it is more generic.
The non-template function.
The compiler reports an ambiguity error.
The compiler selects one randomly.
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution rules state that if a non-template function and a template specialization match a call equally well, the non-template function is always preferred.

mcqs.question: Does Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) occur if the function call is fully qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)`)?
options: Yes, ADL searches namespaces associated with the type of `x`.
No, ADL is only performed for unqualified function calls.
Yes, but only if `x` is a user-defined type.
No, qualified calls are handled entirely at link time.
mcqs.explanation: Argument-Dependent Lookup (ADL) only applies to unqualified names (e.g. `foo(x)`). If the call is qualified (e.g. `std::foo(x)` or `MyLib::foo(x)`), the compiler uses normal lookup rules and bypasses ADL completely.

subtopics.title: RAII and PIMPL Idiom
subtopics.explanation:
**RAII** (covered in Day 3) is C++'s most important idiom. **PIMPL** (Pointer to IMPLementation) hides implementation details behind a pointer to a forward-declared class. Benefits: reduces compilation dependencies (changes to implementation don't require recompiling users), maintains ABI stability (the pointer size doesn't change when implementation changes).

**PIMPL** pattern: public header declares only a `unique_ptr<Impl>` member. The Impl class is defined only in the .cpp file. Constructor, destructor, copy/move must be in the .cpp (where Impl is complete).

### Unforgettable Analogy / Deep Dive
**RAII** is like a rental car agreement: the moment you sign the keys (constructor), you own the car, and the moment you return the keys (destructor), you release it. The resource's lifetime is bound to the lifespan of the stack object. If the stack unwinds due to an exception or scope exit, C++ guarantees that the destructor is called automatically, preventing resource leaks.

examples.title: PIMPL Pattern
examples.explanation: PIMPL hides implementation, reduces compilation deps, maintains ABI.

pitfalls: Forgetting to define destructor in .cpp — unique_ptr needs complete type for deletion
**PIMPL** adds heap allocation and indirection overhead
Not providing move operations — unique_ptr member makes class move-only
tips_to_remember: **PIMPL** = ABI stability + reduced compile deps + true encapsulation
Destructor and move operations MUST be in .cpp where Impl is defined
**PIMPL** adds one indirection per method call — negligible for most uses

questions.question: What is PIMPL and when should you use it?
questions.answer: PIMPL hides implementation behind a unique_ptr to a forward-declared struct. Use for: ABI stability (shared libraries), reducing compilation dependencies (heavy headers), hiding platform-specific implementation. Cost: one heap allocation + one indirection per call.

questions.question: Why must the destructor be in the .cpp file with PIMPL?
questions.answer: unique_ptr's destructor needs to see the complete Impl type to call delete. In the header, Impl is only forward-declared (incomplete). The destructor must be defined in the .cpp where struct Impl is fully defined.

mcqs.question: What happens when you pass an array `int arr[10]` to a function declared as `void process(int arr[])`?
options: The array is passed by value, making a copy of all 10 integers.
It decays to a raw pointer `int*`, and its size information is lost.
The compiler verifies the size is exactly 10 and throws a warning if not.
It is passed as a safe reference to the array.
mcqs.explanation: Arrays passed to functions decay to pointers. Inside `process`, `arr` is a raw pointer (`int*`), and `sizeof(arr)` returns the pointer size (e.g. 8 bytes), not the array size.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a compiler error for `std::unique_ptr`?
options: Moving it using `std::move`.
Attempting to copy it via copy assignment or copy constructor.
Resetting it using `.reset()`.
Releasing ownership with `.release()`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::unique_ptr` represents exclusive ownership. To prevent duplicate owners, copying is disabled (deleted copy constructor/assignment), causing a compilation error.

mcqs.question: What is the outcome of a circular dependency where two objects contain `std::shared_ptr` pointing to each other?
options: The compiler reports a cyclic template dependency error.
The reference counts will never drop to zero, leaking both objects.
The destructors are called normally due to automatic cycle detection.
The program crashes with a stack overflow on deletion.
mcqs.explanation: Because each object holds a `std::shared_ptr` to the other, their reference counts remain at least 1, even after all external pointers are destroyed, leaking the memory.

mcqs.question: How do you access the managed object of a `std::weak_ptr`?
options: Dereference it directly using `*` or `->`.
You must call `.lock()` to obtain a `std::shared_ptr` first.
Call `.get()` to retrieve the raw pointer.
It is not possible to access the object once it is in a weak pointer.
mcqs.explanation: `std::weak_ptr` does not provide direct access. You must call `.lock()` which returns a `std::shared_ptr`. If the managed object has already been destroyed, the returned shared pointer will be empty.

mcqs.question: What is the primary benefit of using `std::make_shared` instead of `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
options: It makes the shared pointer thread-safe.
It performs a single memory allocation for both the control block and the object, improving performance and cache locality.
It allows using custom delete functions.
It prevents compile-time template instantiation overhead.
mcqs.explanation: `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)` allocates the object first, then allocates the control block. `std::make_shared` allocates a single block of memory big enough to hold both, reducing heap allocation overhead.

mcqs.question: How does a custom deleter function pointer affect the size of a `std::unique_ptr`?
options: It does not affect the size; it remains 8 bytes.
It increases the size of the pointer (typically to 16 bytes) because it must store the function pointer.
It causes the unique_ptr to allocate memory on the heap.
It is a compile-time construct and does not exist at runtime.
mcqs.explanation: If a custom deleter is a function pointer, the unique_ptr must store it, increasing its size. Using a stateless functor (like a lambda with no captures) avoids this size overhead.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of placement `new` in C++?
options: It automatically finds the best place in the heap to allocate memory.
It constructs an object on a pre-allocated raw memory buffer without allocating new heap memory.
It moves an object to another thread's stack space.
It optimizes memory alignment dynamically.
mcqs.explanation: Placement `new` (e.g. `new (buffer) MyClass()`) constructs an object at a specific, pre-allocated memory address, avoiding heap allocation costs.

mcqs.question: How must you destroy an object constructed via placement `new`?
options: Call `delete ptr;`.
Explicitly call the object's destructor (`ptr->~T()`) and then manually manage the buffer's memory.
Let it go out of scope; the stack automatically deletes it.
Call `free(ptr);`.
mcqs.explanation: Because placement `new` did not allocate memory from the global heap, calling `delete` is undefined behavior. You must explicitly invoke the destructor and then clean up the raw buffer.

mcqs.question: What is the undefined behavior hazard in the code `int* p = new int[10]; delete p;`?
options: Using the wrong delete operator (`delete` instead of `delete[]`) is Undefined Behavior.
There is no hazard; `delete` automatically knows it is an array.
It is a compiler error and won't compile.
It causes a stack overflow.
mcqs.explanation: Memory allocated with `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`. Using plain `delete` on an array pointer is undefined behavior, often causing heap corruption or failing to call destructors for elements 1 to 9.

mcqs.question: What is the risk of returning a local variable by reference `const int&` from a function?
options: It copies the variable unnecessarily.
The local variable is destroyed at function exit, leaving a dangling reference, and accessing it is UB.
It compiles only if the variable is marked `static`.
It causes a memory leak on the stack.
mcqs.explanation: Local variables have automatic storage duration (stack-allocated) and are destroyed when the function returns. Accessing a reference to a destroyed local variable is undefined behavior.

subtopics.title: Classic GoF Patterns in C++ — Singleton, Factory, Observer, Strategy, Visitor
subtopics.explanation: Singleton: exactly one instance. Meyer's Singleton (function-`static`) is thread-safe since C++11. Factory: creates objects without specifying exact types. Observer: event notification pattern. Strategy: interchangeable algorithms. Visitor: double dispatch for operations on variant types — modernized with `std::visit` + `std::variant` in C++17.

examples.title: Modern Patterns
examples.explanation: Meyer's Singleton is thread-safe. std::visit replaces traditional Visitor pattern.

pitfalls: Singleton overuse — it's essentially a global variable with extra steps
Factory returning raw pointers — return unique_ptr instead
Observer holding raw pointers to subjects — use weak_ptr for safety
tips_to_remember: Singletons are often an anti-pattern — consider dependency injection
Return unique_ptr from factories, not raw pointers
`std::variant` + `std::visit` is the modern Visitor — no `virtual` dispatch needed
Strategy pattern = just pass a callable (lambda, `std::function`)

questions.question: What is Meyer's Singleton?
questions.answer: A Singleton using a function-static variable: static T& instance() { static T obj; return obj; }. Thread-safe since C++11 (magic statics guarantee). Lazy initialization. Simple and correct.

questions.question: How does std::variant replace the Visitor pattern?
questions.answer: Traditional Visitor requires virtual functions and double dispatch. std::variant<Types...> with std::visit provides the same functionality: pattern matching on a closed set of types, but without inheritance, vtables, or heap allocation.

mcqs.question: What action invalidates all active iterators of a `std::vector`?
options: Modifying an element inside the vector.
An insertion that causes the vector to exceed its current `capacity()`, triggering memory reallocation.
Calling `.reserve()` with a value smaller than the current capacity.
Iterating through the vector in reverse order.
mcqs.explanation: If a vector grows beyond its `capacity()`, it allocates a new larger heap block, copies elements over, and frees the old block. All pointers, references, and iterators pointing to the old memory become invalid (dangling).

mcqs.question: What is the average search complexity of `std::unordered_map` vs `std::map`?
options: O(n) vs O(1)
O(1) (hash table lookup) vs O(log n) (balanced binary tree traversal).
O(log n) vs O(n log n)
They have the same complexity.
mcqs.explanation: `std::unordered_map` uses a hash table, providing O(1) average search complexity. `std::map` uses a red-black tree, requiring O(log n) comparisons.

mcqs.question: Why is `std::vector<bool>` space-optimized, and what is its major drawback?
options: It uses compression algorithms, making it slow.
It packs elements as single bits (1 bit per bool), but since bits are not addressable, it cannot return a standard `bool&` reference, returning a proxy instead.
It cannot be resized after construction.
It is a compile-time constant array.
mcqs.explanation: To save space, `std::vector<bool>` stores 8 booleans per byte. Because C++ cannot reference sub-byte memory bits, `operator[]` returns a proxy object (`std::vector<bool>::reference`) instead of `bool&`, which can break generic code.

mcqs.question: Why does calling `std::sort` on a `std::list` result in a compilation error?
options: `std::list` cannot be sorted.
`std::sort` requires random-access iterators; `std::list` only provides bidirectional iterators. You must use `std::list::sort()` instead.
`std::list` elements are constant.
You must include `<list_sort>`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::sort` uses algorithms that require random-access iterators (like `std::vector` or arrays). `std::list` is a doubly linked list and only supports bidirectional traversal, so you must use the container-specific member `.sort()`.

mcqs.question: What is the primary danger of using `std::string_view` in `Classic GoF Patterns in C++ — Singleton, Factory, Observer, Strategy, Visitor`?
options: It copies strings, reducing performance.
It is a non-owning view; if the underlying string object is destroyed (e.g. temporary string), the `string_view` becomes a dangling pointer.
It cannot be converted to `std::string`.
It requires compile-time evaluation.
mcqs.explanation: `std::string_view` stores a pointer and a length. It does not own the characters. If the owner string is modified, moved, or destroyed, the `string_view` refers to invalid memory.

mcqs.question: Does calling the `std::remove` algorithm actually erase elements and resize a container?
options: Yes, it removes elements and changes the container size.
No, it only shifts the elements to the front and returns an iterator to the new logical end; you must call the container's `.erase()` to resize it (Erase-Remove idiom).
No, it is a compile-time check only.
Yes, but only for `std::list`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::remove` operates on iterators and cannot access the container's size properties. It moves elements to the front, leaving the container size unchanged. You must call `.erase(new_end, end)` to delete the trailing elements.

mcqs.question: What does C++23 `std::expected<T, E>` represent?
options: A template class that estimates execution time.
A vocabulary type that holds either a success value of type `T` or an error value of type `E` (unexpected), replacing exceptions for expected errors.
A replacement for `std::future`.
An optimizer flag.
mcqs.explanation: `std::expected` provides functional error handling. It returns either the success result or the error payload in a single type-safe object, avoiding exception-handling overhead for predictable failures.

mcqs.question: What is a `std::span` introduced in C++20?
options: A wrapper that runs objects across multiple CPU cores.
A non-owning view over a contiguous sequence of elements (like an array or vector), storing a pointer and a size.
A compiler instruction for thread interference size.
A class that measures time spans.
mcqs.explanation: `std::span` is a lightweight, non-owning view that provides safe, contiguous access to arrays, vectors, or buffers without copying data or depending on specific container types.

mcqs.question: What happens if a lambda captures a local variable by reference `[&]`, and is executed after the variable goes out of scope?
options: The lambda copies the variable before destruction.
Accessing the reference triggers Undefined Behavior because it points to a destroyed stack variable.
The compiler extends the variable's lifetime automatically.
It is a compile-time error.
mcqs.explanation: Capturing by reference `[&]` does not extend the lifetime of stack variables. If the lambda executes after the variable goes out of scope, it is a dangling reference and accessing it is undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: What category is returned by the C++20 spaceship operator `<=>` for floating-point comparisons?
options: `std::strong_ordering`
`std::weak_ordering`
`std::partial_ordering` (because `NaN` is unordered)
`std::float_ordering`
mcqs.explanation: Floating-point numbers can represent `NaN` (Not a Number). Since `NaN` cannot be compared to other numbers (`NaN < 1` is false, and `NaN > 1` is false), comparisons are partially ordered, returning `std::partial_ordering`.

subtopics.title: Type Erasure
subtopics.explanation:
Type erasure allows storing objects of different types behind a common interface without inheritance. `std::function` is the canonical example — it wraps any callable (lambda, function pointer, functor) behind a uniform type.

Implementation: a base class with `virtual` methods holds the type-erased interface. A templated derived class wraps the concrete type. The outer class holds a unique_ptr to the base. Small Buffer Optimization (SBO) avoids heap allocation for small types.

examples.title: Custom Type Erasure
examples.explanation: Type erasure: interface via base class, storage via templated derived class, hidden behind a value type.

pitfalls: Type erasure adds heap allocation and `virtual` dispatch overhead
Not implementing SBO for small callables (`std::function` does this)
Losing type information makes debugging harder
tips_to_remember: Type erasure = value semantics + `virtual` dispatch hidden behind a facade
`std::function`, `std::any`, and `std::move_only_function` all use type erasure
SBO (Small Buffer Optimization) avoids heap for small types

questions.question: What is type erasure?
questions.answer: A technique to store objects of arbitrary types behind a common, non-template interface. The type information is 'erased' at compile time but the correct behavior is preserved through virtual dispatch internally. std::function is the most common example.

questions.question: How does type erasure differ from inheritance?
questions.answer: With inheritance, the user writes the derived class and passes pointers/references. With type erasure, the wrapping class internally creates the derived class — the user just passes any conforming object by value. The user doesn't need to inherit from anything.

subtopics.title: Bitwise Operations & Bit-Fields
subtopics.explanation:
Bitwise operators: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT), << (left shift), >> (right shift). Used for flags, masks, hardware registers, and compact data storage. Bit-fields allow specifying the number of bits for struct members: struct { unsigned flag : 1; unsigned value : 4; }.

Common idiom: flags with enum class and bitwise operators.

examples.title: Bitwise Operations
examples.explanation: Bitwise ops for flags. Bit-fields for compact storage.

pitfalls: Right-shifting signed integers is implementation-defined (arithmetic vs logical)
Bit-field layout (order, padding) is implementation-defined — not portable for serialization
Shifting by >= bit-width is UB
tips_to_remember: Use unsigned types for bitwise operations
Bit-field layout is not portable — don't use for network/file formats
Prefer enum class with operator overloads for type-safe flags

questions.question: Are bit-fields portable?
questions.answer: No. The layout of bit-fields (order, padding, signedness) is implementation-defined. Different compilers may arrange them differently. Don't use bit-fields for cross-platform serialization or hardware register mapping — use explicit shifts and masks instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between arithmetic and logical right shift?
questions.answer: Arithmetic shift (signed) preserves the sign bit (fills with 1 for negative). Logical shift (unsigned) fills with 0. C++ right-shift of negative integers is implementation-defined.

mcqs.question: Why is `std::vector<bool>` space-optimized, and what is its major drawback?
options: It uses compression algorithms, making it slow.
It packs elements as single bits (1 bit per bool), but since bits are not addressable, it cannot return a standard `bool&` reference, returning a proxy instead.
It cannot be resized after construction.
It is a compile-time constant array.
mcqs.explanation: To save space, `std::vector<bool>` stores 8 booleans per byte. Because C++ cannot reference sub-byte memory bits, `operator[]` returns a proxy object (`std::vector<bool>::reference`) instead of `bool&`, which can break generic code.

mcqs.question: Why does calling `std::sort` on a `std::list` result in a compilation error?
options: `std::list` cannot be sorted.
`std::sort` requires random-access iterators; `std::list` only provides bidirectional iterators. You must use `std::list::sort()` instead.
`std::list` elements are constant.
You must include `<list_sort>`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::sort` uses algorithms that require random-access iterators (like `std::vector` or arrays). `std::list` is a doubly linked list and only supports bidirectional traversal, so you must use the container-specific member `.sort()`.

mcqs.question: What is the primary danger of using `std::string_view` in `Bitwise Operations & Bit-Fields`?
options: It copies strings, reducing performance.
It is a non-owning view; if the underlying string object is destroyed (e.g. temporary string), the `string_view` becomes a dangling pointer.
It cannot be converted to `std::string`.
It requires compile-time evaluation.
mcqs.explanation: `std::string_view` stores a pointer and a length. It does not own the characters. If the owner string is modified, moved, or destroyed, the `string_view` refers to invalid memory.

mcqs.question: Does calling the `std::remove` algorithm actually erase elements and resize a container?
options: Yes, it removes elements and changes the container size.
No, it only shifts the elements to the front and returns an iterator to the new logical end; you must call the container's `.erase()` to resize it (Erase-Remove idiom).
No, it is a compile-time check only.
Yes, but only for `std::list`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::remove` operates on iterators and cannot access the container's size properties. It moves elements to the front, leaving the container size unchanged. You must call `.erase(new_end, end)` to delete the trailing elements.

mcqs.question: What does C++23 `std::expected<T, E>` represent?
options: A template class that estimates execution time.
A vocabulary type that holds either a success value of type `T` or an error value of type `E` (unexpected), replacing exceptions for expected errors.
A replacement for `std::future`.
An optimizer flag.
mcqs.explanation: `std::expected` provides functional error handling. It returns either the success result or the error payload in a single type-safe object, avoiding exception-handling overhead for predictable failures.

mcqs.question: What is a `std::span` introduced in C++20?
options: A wrapper that runs objects across multiple CPU cores.
A non-owning view over a contiguous sequence of elements (like an array or vector), storing a pointer and a size.
A compiler instruction for thread interference size.
A class that measures time spans.
mcqs.explanation: `std::span` is a lightweight, non-owning view that provides safe, contiguous access to arrays, vectors, or buffers without copying data or depending on specific container types.

mcqs.question: What happens if a lambda captures a local variable by reference `[&]`, and is executed after the variable goes out of scope?
options: The lambda copies the variable before destruction.
Accessing the reference triggers Undefined Behavior because it points to a destroyed stack variable.
The compiler extends the variable's lifetime automatically.
It is a compile-time error.
mcqs.explanation: Capturing by reference `[&]` does not extend the lifetime of stack variables. If the lambda executes after the variable goes out of scope, it is a dangling reference and accessing it is undefined behavior.

mcqs.question: What category is returned by the C++20 spaceship operator `<=>` for floating-point comparisons?
options: `std::strong_ordering`
`std::weak_ordering`
`std::partial_ordering` (because `NaN` is unordered)
`std::float_ordering`
mcqs.explanation: Floating-point numbers can represent `NaN` (Not a Number). Since `NaN` cannot be compared to other numbers (`NaN < 1` is false, and `NaN > 1` is false), comparisons are partially ordered, returning `std::partial_ordering`.

subtopics.title: Endianness
subtopics.explanation:
Byte order: how multi-byte values are stored in memory. Little-endian (x86, ARM default): least significant byte first. Big-endian (network byte order, some ARM modes): most significant byte first.

Endianness matters for: network protocols (always big-endian by convention), file formats, cross-platform serialization. Use `ntohl`/`htonl` for network byte order conversion. C++20 adds `std::endian` for compile-time endianness detection.

examples.title: Endianness
examples.explanation: Use htonl/ntohl for network byte order. std::endian (C++20) for detection.

pitfalls: Assuming endianness — code breaks on different architectures
Not converting byte order in network protocols — garbled data
Type-punning to check endianness (UB) instead of using `std::endian`
tips_to_remember: Network byte order is always big-endian — use `htonl`/`ntohl`
x86/x64 is always little-endian. ARM can be either.
C++20 `std::endian::native` tells you at compile time

questions.question: When does endianness matter?
questions.answer: Network protocols (TCP/IP uses big-endian), file format reading/writing, cross-platform data exchange, hardware register access. For local computation it's invisible.

questions.question: How do you handle endianness in portable code?
questions.answer: Use htonl/ntohl/htons/ntohs for network byte order conversion. Use std::endian (C++20) for compile-time detection. Write serialization code that explicitly specifies byte order.

mcqs.question: What action invalidates all active iterators of a `std::vector`?
options: Modifying an element inside the vector.
An insertion that causes the vector to exceed its current `capacity()`, triggering memory reallocation.
Calling `.reserve()` with a value smaller than the current capacity.
Iterating through the vector in reverse order.
mcqs.explanation: If a vector grows beyond its `capacity()`, it allocates a new larger heap block, copies elements over, and frees the old block. All pointers, references, and iterators pointing to the old memory become invalid (dangling).

mcqs.question: What is the average search complexity of `std::unordered_map` vs `std::map`?
options: O(n) vs O(1)
O(1) (hash table lookup) vs O(log n) (balanced binary tree traversal).
O(log n) vs O(n log n)
They have the same complexity.
mcqs.explanation: `std::unordered_map` uses a hash table, providing O(1) average search complexity. `std::map` uses a red-black tree, requiring O(log n) comparisons.

subtopics.title: volatile vs atomic
subtopics.explanation:
`volatile` tells the compiler not to optimize away reads/writes to a variable — every access goes to memory. It does NOT provide atomicity or synchronization. It's for memory-mapped I/O, signal handlers, and setjmp/longjmp.

`std::atomic` provides atomicity AND synchronization (with memory ordering). For multithreading, always use atomic, never `volatile`. `volatile` atomic exists but is rarely needed.

examples.title: volatile vs atomic
examples.explanation: volatile = don't optimize away. atomic = thread-safe. They serve different purposes.

pitfalls: Using `volatile` for thread synchronization — it provides NO atomicity
Assuming `volatile` prevents reordering — it doesn't (only compiler, not CPU)
Java's `volatile` ≠ C++'s `volatile` (Java's `volatile` IS like C++'s atomic)
tips_to_remember: `volatile` = hardware/signal handler use ONLY. atomic = multithreading.
`volatile` prevents compiler optimizations. atomic prevents compiler AND CPU reordering.
In C++, `volatile` has nothing to do with threads

questions.question: What is the difference between volatile and atomic?
questions.answer: volatile prevents the compiler from optimizing away reads/writes (for hardware registers, signal handlers). atomic provides atomicity and synchronization for multithreading. volatile does NOT make operations atomic or provide any threading guarantees.

questions.question: When should you use volatile?
questions.answer: Memory-mapped I/O (hardware registers), signal handlers (volatile sig_atomic_t), setjmp/longjmp. Never for multithreading — use std::atomic instead.

mcqs.question: What is the key difference between `std::thread` and `std::jthread` (C++20) on destruction?
options: `std::jthread` allocates thread resources on the stack.
`std::jthread` automatically joins and requests cooperative interruption on destruction, while `std::thread` calls `std::terminate` if it is still joinable.
`std::thread` is faster to construct.
`std::jthread` does not support lambda execution.
mcqs.explanation: If a `std::thread` is destroyed while it is still joinable (running and not joined/detached), it calls `std::terminate`, crashing the program. `std::jthread` automatically joins and cooperatively signals stop on destruction.

mcqs.question: What constitutes a data race in C++?
options: Two threads executing different functions simultaneously.
Two or more threads accessing the same memory location concurrently, where at least one access is a write, and without synchronization.
Using global variables in a multithreaded application.
When a thread fails to acquire a lock in time.
mcqs.explanation: A data race is defined as concurrent unsynchronized access to the same memory location where at least one thread is writing. Data races are undefined behavior in C++.

mcqs.question: Why would you prefer `std::unique_lock` over `std::lock_guard`?
options: `std::unique_lock` is faster.
`std::unique_lock` provides advanced features like deferring lock, explicit unlocking, timeout locking, and move semantics, whereas `std::lock_guard` is strictly scoped.
`std::lock_guard` causes deadlocks easily.
`std::unique_lock` does not require a mutex reference.
mcqs.explanation: `std::lock_guard` is a simple, zero-overhead wrapper for basic scoped locking. `std::unique_lock` has a small overhead but supports complex use cases like deferred locking, manual unlocking, and transferring locks.

mcqs.question: How does `std::scoped_lock` (C++17) prevent deadlocks when locking multiple mutexes?
options: It compiles the mutexes into a single lock.
It uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm to lock all passed mutexes simultaneously.
It runs a background thread to monitor locks.
It converts mutexes to atomic variables.
mcqs.explanation: `std::scoped_lock` can lock multiple mutexes. It uses the same deadlock avoidance algorithm as `std::lock` under the hood, ensuring they are acquired in a safe, sorted sequence.

mcqs.question: What is the key benefit of `std::atomic` variables?
options: They make entire classes thread-safe.
Operations on them are guaranteed to be atomic, preventing data races without needing a heavy mutex lock.
They run code on separate CPU cores.
They prevent memory allocations.
mcqs.explanation: Operations on `std::atomic` variables are executed as single, indivisible CPU instructions, ensuring thread safety and preventing data races without the system-call overhead of mutexes.

mcqs.question: What is the default memory order for atomic operations in C++?
options: `std::memory_order_relaxed`
`std::memory_order_seq_cst` (Sequential Consistency)
`std::memory_order_acquire`
`std::memory_order_release`
mcqs.explanation: By default, all atomic operations use `std::memory_order_seq_cst`. This provides sequential consistency, establishing a global, total ordering of all operations visible to all threads.

mcqs.question: What guarantees does `std::memory_order_relaxed` provide?
options: It guarantees that operations are atomic, but provides no synchronization or ordering guarantees for surrounding memory accesses.
It behaves exactly like sequentially consistent order but runs faster.
It locks the CPU caches during execution.
It is a runtime check that throws an exception on race.
mcqs.explanation: `memory_order_relaxed` only guarantees atomicity of the variable itself. The compiler and CPU are free to reorder surrounding read/write instructions around it, providing no synchronization between threads.

mcqs.question: Why must a condition variable wait loop check the predicate condition (e.g. `cv.wait(lock, []{ return ready; })`)?
options: To yield the CPU back to the OS.
To prevent spurious wakeups, where the thread wakes up without receiving a signal.
Because condition variables can only wake up once.
To register the thread with the scheduler.
mcqs.explanation: Condition variables are subject to 'spurious wakeups' due to OS implementation details. A thread can wake up even if no signal was sent. Thus, the thread must always re-verify the predicate condition.

mcqs.question: What is the relationship between `std::promise` and `std::future`?
options: They are synonyms for the same class.
`std::promise` sets a value or exception in a shared state, which `std::future` retrieves asynchronously.
`std::future` is used to send values, `std::promise` is used to read them.
They are used to create recursive mutex locks.
mcqs.explanation: A promise is the writer-end and a future is the reader-end of an asynchronous channel. `std::promise` writes a value or exception to the shared channel state, which is retrieved via `std::future::get()`.

mcqs.question: Does the `volatile` keyword provide thread synchronization or atomicity in C++?
options: Yes, it makes variables thread-safe.
No, `volatile` only prevents compiler register caching optimizations for hardware registers; it does NOT prevent data races or guarantee thread memory order.
Yes, it acts as a lightweight atomic variable.
No, it is a deprecated keyword in modern C++.
mcqs.explanation: Unlike Java/C#, `volatile` in C++ has nothing to do with multithreading. It only instructs the compiler not to optimize away reads/writes to memory (useful for memory-mapped I/O). It does not generate atomic CPU operations or memory barriers.

subtopics.title: C++11 — The Modern C++ Revolution
subtopics.explanation:
C++11 was the biggest evolution of C++: auto type deduction, lambdas, move semantics (&&, `std::move`), smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr), range-for loops, `nullptr`, `constexpr`, variadic templates, `std::thread`, `std::atomic`, enum class, `static_assert`, `decltype`, initializer lists.

This was when 'Modern C++' began. Almost all new C++ code should use C++11 features as a baseline.

examples.title: C++11 Highlights
examples.code:
auto x = 42;                           // auto deduction
auto v = std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3};    // initializer list
for (auto& item : v) item *= 2;        // range-for

auto ptr = std::make_unique<int>(42);   // smart pointer
auto fn = [](int x) { return x * 2; }; // lambda

std::string s = "hello";
auto s2 = std::move(s);                 // move semantics

enum class Color { Red, Green, Blue };  // scoped enum
constexpr int sq(int n) { return n*n; };// constexpr
examples.explanation: C++11 introduced the foundation of modern C++.

pitfalls: Overusing auto when the type isn't obvious — hurts readability
Forgetting `std::move` returns an xvalue, not a moved object
Using NULL instead of `nullptr`
tips_to_remember: C++11 is the baseline for modern C++
auto, lambdas, move semantics, smart pointers, range-for — use them everywhere
`nullptr` replaces NULL. enum class replaces enum.

questions.question: What are the most important C++11 features?
questions.answer: Move semantics (performance), smart pointers (safety), lambdas (expressiveness), auto (convenience), range-for (readability), constexpr (compile-time), nullptr (type safety), variadic templates (generic programming), threads/atomics (standard concurrency).

questions.question: Why was C++11 so significant?
questions.answer: It modernized C++ from a language stuck in 1998. It added: zero-cost abstractions (move semantics), safety (smart pointers, nullptr), expressiveness (lambdas, auto, range-for), and standardized concurrency (threads, atomics).

subtopics.title: C++14/17 — Refinements and Vocabulary Types
subtopics.explanation:
C++14: generic lambdas (auto parameters), relaxed `constexpr` (loops, local vars), variable templates, `std::make_unique`, binary literals (0b1010), digit separators (1'000'000).

C++17: structured bindings (auto [x,y] = pair), if `constexpr`, `std::optional`/variant/any, parallel STL algorithms, `std::filesystem`, fold expressions, `inline` variables, class `template` argument deduction (**CTAD**), `std::string_view`, nested namespaces (`A::B::C`), [[nodiscard]], [[maybe_unused]].

examples.title: C++17 Highlights
examples.explanation: C++17 added vocabulary types, compile-time branching, and parallel STL.

pitfalls: Assuming if `constexpr` removes code — it's still parsed, just not instantiated
string_view dangling: creating string_view from a temporary string
Parallel algorithms need TBB or similar backend
tips_to_remember: C++14: relaxed `constexpr` + generic lambdas = more expressive templates
C++17: structured bindings + optional/variant + if `constexpr` = huge readability wins
`inline` variables solve the 'define in header' problem for constants

questions.question: What is if constexpr?
questions.answer: Compile-time branching: if constexpr (condition) { ... } else { ... }. The false branch is not instantiated (for templates). This replaces SFINAE and tag dispatch for many use cases.

questions.question: What are structured bindings?
questions.answer: auto [a, b, c] = tuple_or_struct; — unpacks aggregates, tuples, pairs, and arrays into named variables. Much cleaner than std::get<0>(tuple).

mcqs.question: What is a `std::span` introduced in C++20?

A compiler instruction for thread interference size.
A class that measures time spans.

mcqs.question: What happens if a lambda captures a local variable by reference `[&]`, and is executed after the variable goes out of scope?

mcqs.question: What category is returned by the C++20 spaceship operator `<=>` for floating-point comparisons?

questions.question: What are C++20 ranges?

questions.question: What is the spaceship operator?
questions.answer: auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default; generates all six comparison operators (<, <=, ==, !=, >=, >) from one declaration. Returns an ordering category (strong_ordering, weak_ordering, partial_ordering).

mcqs.question: When does template instantiation occur in C++?
options: At runtime, when the function is called.
At compile time, when the template is instantiated with concrete types.
At link time, when symbols are resolved.
During preprocessing.
mcqs.explanation: Templates are compile-time constructs. The compiler generates concrete class or function code (instantiation) during compilation when it sees the template used with specific type arguments.

mcqs.question: What is SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error) in C++ templates?
options: A compiler flag that ignores all syntax errors inside templates.
A rule stating that if a substitution failure occurs during overload candidate resolution, the candidate is discarded without causing a compilation error.
A template debugging tool.
A C++20 feature that replaces concepts.
mcqs.explanation: SFINAE states that if a type substitution fails while inspecting overloaded templates, it does not stop compilation. The compiler simply removes that candidate from the overload set and keeps searching.

mcqs.question: How do you define an explicit template specialization for class `Box` with type `int`?
options: `template<int> class Box { ... };`
`template<> class Box<int> { ... };`
`template class Box<int>;`
`specialized class Box<int> { ... };`
mcqs.explanation: Explicit (or full) template specialization is declared with `template<>` followed by the class definition specifying the type in brackets: `class Box<int> { ... };`.

mcqs.question: Why is the `typename` keyword required before a nested dependent name (e.g. `typename T::iterator`) in templates?
options: It is a hint to the compiler to inline the type.
To resolve ambiguity, informing the compiler that the name refers to a nested type rather than a static member variable.
To import the type into the namespace.
It is only required in C++98, not modern C++.
mcqs.explanation: Because `T` is a template parameter, the compiler cannot inspect it during the first phase of template parsing. It assumes nested names are static members unless prefixed with `typename` to signify a type.

mcqs.question: How does `std::enable_if` conditionally enable templates?
options: It throws a compilation warning if the condition is false.
It uses SFINAE: if the condition is false, the nested type does not exist, causing substitution to fail and candidate discard.
It is a runtime check that throws an exception.
It disables optimizer passes for the template.
mcqs.explanation: `std::enable_if_t<Cond, T>` defines a nested `type` equal to `T` only if `Cond` is true. If `Cond` is false, it has no nested type, triggering a substitution failure (SFINAE) and excluding the template from overload resolution.

mcqs.question: What is the expanded result of the C++17 fold expression `(... + args)` where `args` is `1, 2, 3`?
options: `1 + 2 + 3` (flat summation)
It is invalid syntax.
mcqs.explanation: `(... + args)` is a unary left fold. It expands starting from the left: `((1 + 2) + 3)`. A right fold is `(args + ...)` which expands to `(1 + (2 + 3))`.

mcqs.question: What happens if a template argument fails to satisfy a C++20 `concept` constraint (e.g. `requires std::integral<T>`)?
options: The compiler falls back to runtime type checks.
It produces a clean compilation error at the call site, listing which constraint failed.
The compiler ignores the template and uses default arguments.
It triggers undefined behavior.
mcqs.explanation: C++20 concepts replace complex template SFINAE hacks with clear, readable constraint requirements. If constraint checks fail, the compiler outputs a clean, readable error explaining exactly which constraint was violated.

mcqs.question: Can you partially specialize a function template in C++?
options: Yes, using the standard `template<typename T> void f<T*>()` syntax.
No, function templates can only be fully specialized; you must use function overloading instead.
Yes, but only inside namespaces.
Yes, if the return type is `auto`.
mcqs.explanation: C++ does not allow partial specialization of function templates. If you need to partially specialize a function template, you must use function overloading or delegate to a helper class template.

mcqs.question: What is two-phase lookup in template compilation?
options: The compiler parses the template once for syntax, and once for linkage.
Non-dependent names are checked in phase 1 (definition); dependent names are checked in phase 2 (instantiation).
It is a runtime optimization phase.
The compiler compiles the header first, then the source.
mcqs.explanation: During phase 1, the compiler parses the template and checks all names that do not depend on template parameters. During phase 2 (when the template is instantiated with actual types), the compiler resolves all dependent names.

mcqs.question: What is Class Template Argument Deduction (CTAD) introduced in C++17?
options: It allows class templates to inherit template arguments from base classes.
It allows the compiler to deduce class template parameters from constructor arguments, avoiding explicit template parameters.
It compiles templates faster by caching template types.
It is a dynamic cast for templates.
mcqs.explanation: CTAD allows writing `std::pair p(1, 2.5)` instead of `std::pair<int, double> p(1, 2.5)`. The compiler automatically infers the template types by inspecting constructor parameters.

subtopics.title: Coroutines — co_await, co_yield, co_return
subtopics.explanation:
Coroutines (C++20) are functions that can suspend and resume, enabling asynchronous and generator-style code without threads. A coroutine is any function containing `co_await`, `co_yield`, or `co_return`. The compiler transforms it into a state machine, allocating a coroutine frame on the heap to hold suspended state.

Key concepts: `co_await` suspends until an awaiter is ready; `co_yield` produces a value in a generator; `co_return` returns from the coroutine. The return type must be a coroutine type (e.g. `std::generator<T>` in C++23, or a custom task type). Coroutines are the foundation for async I/O, lazy generators, and cooperative multitasking.

C++23 adds `std::generator<T>` which dramatically simplifies writing generators — you just write a function with `co_yield` and it becomes an iterable range.

examples.title: Coroutine Generator (C++23)
examples.explanation: std::generator (C++23) makes coroutine generators trivial — co_yield produces values lazily.

pitfalls: Forgetting that coroutine frames are heap-allocated — can be a performance concern

A coroutine that never suspends still allocates a frame
Debugging coroutines is harder — the stack is split across suspension points

`std::generator<T>` (C++23) is the easy way to write generators

questions.question: What is a coroutine?
questions.answer: A function that can suspend and resume. It contains co_await, co_yield, or co_return. The compiler transforms it into a state machine with a heap-allocated frame. Coroutines enable async I/O and lazy generators without threads.

questions.question: What is the difference between co_await and co_yield?
questions.answer: co_await suspends the coroutine until an asynchronous operation completes (used in async/task coroutines). co_yield produces a value and suspends, used in generator coroutines to lazily produce a sequence of values.

questions.question: What does std::generator do in C++23?
questions.answer: std::generator<T> is a standard coroutine type that makes writing generators trivial. A function returning std::generator<T> that uses co_yield becomes a lazily-evaluated, iterable range — no manual coroutine boilerplate needed.

mcqs.question: What action invalidates all active iterators of a `std::vector`?
options: Modifying an element inside the vector.
An insertion that causes the vector to exceed its current `capacity()`, triggering memory reallocation.
Calling `.reserve()` with a value smaller than the current capacity.
Iterating through the vector in reverse order.
mcqs.explanation: If a vector grows beyond its `capacity()`, it allocates a new larger heap block, copies elements over, and frees the old block. All pointers, references, and iterators pointing to the old memory become invalid (dangling).

mcqs.question: What is the average search complexity of `std::unordered_map` vs `std::map`?
options: O(n) vs O(1)
O(1) (hash table lookup) vs O(log n) (balanced binary tree traversal).
O(log n) vs O(n log n)
They have the same complexity.
mcqs.explanation: `std::unordered_map` uses a hash table, providing O(1) average search complexity. `std::map` uses a red-black tree, requiring O(log n) comparisons.

mcqs.question: Why is `std::vector<bool>` space-optimized, and what is its major drawback?
options: It uses compression algorithms, making it slow.
It packs elements as single bits (1 bit per bool), but since bits are not addressable, it cannot return a standard `bool&` reference, returning a proxy instead.
It cannot be resized after construction.
It is a compile-time constant array.

mcqs.question: Why does calling `std::sort` on a `std::list` result in a compilation error?

`std::list` elements are constant.
You must include `<list_sort>`.
mcqs.explanation: `std::sort` uses algorithms that require random-access iterators (like `std::vector` or arrays). `std::list` is a doubly linked list and only supports bidirectional traversal, so you must use the container-specific member `.sort()`.

subtopics.title: std::format & std::print — Modern Text Formatting
subtopics.explanation:
`std::format` (C++20) provides type-safe, Python-style string formatting: `std::format`("{} + {} = {}", a, b, a+b). It's faster and safer than printf (no format-string/argument mismatch) and more readable than iostreams. `std::print` (C++23) writes formatted output directly to stdout without stream overhead.

Format specifiers: {:d} integer, {:f} float, {:x} hex, {:>10} right-align width 10, {:.2f} two decimals. `std::format_to` writes into a buffer. `std::formatter<T>` can be specialized for user-defined types.

questions.question: What is the advantage of std::format over printf?

questions.question: What is the difference between std::format and std::print?
